Summary
Very cold ions (H+, He+, O+) in the inner magnetosphere respond to geomagnetic storms through inward convection, acceleration, and charge exchange losses, but the character of these responses differs systematically between CIR‑driven and CME‑driven storms because the two drivers differ in upstream structure, convection strength, and duration. CIRs produce longer, more gradual compressional driving with persistent ring‑current buildup and preferential O+ energization and transport to low L, whereas CMEs deliver brief, stronger impulses that more rapidly increase ring‑current pressure at low L and drive larger enhancements of O+ at smaller L, followed by faster spectral relaxation. <cite id="ea937427-0">CIR-driven and CME-driven storms are distinguished by sustained solar-wind speed increases with plasma-density drops at the stream interface for CIRs, and by brief, dense plasma-sheet inflows and stronger Dst perturbations for CMEs</cite><cite id="ad0987ab-1">CME storms typically feature stronger but shorter-lived magnetospheric convection than CIR storms, while CIR storms have much longer durations despite lower energy input rates</cite><cite id="ea937427-3">CME-driven storms are brief with denser plasma sheets and stronger Dst perturbations, often accompanied by SEPs, whereas CIR-driven storms are longer with hotter plasma sheets and higher relativistic electron fluxes</cite>.

Cold-ion populations and energies: equatorial inner magnetosphere signatures
During storm main phases, equatorial cold/thermal ions show clear spectral and spatial changes: oxygen is preferentially energized and transported inward, with larger phase-space-density (PSD) enhancements than helium and hydrogen at comparable μ, and O+ penetrates deeper to minimum L ≈ 3.6 than higher-μ ions. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">Simultaneous RBSP and Geotail observations during a 17 March 2015 storm show flux enhancements across all three ion species at storm onset, consistent with fresh plasma injection from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere, and indicate preferential acceleration of O+ ions and inward convection from the plasma sheet; RBSP energy-time spectrograms display higher-energy flux enhancements during the main phase</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">In a RBSP-B case study, O+ PSD enhancements exceeded He+ and H+ (S(O+) > S(He+) > S(H+)), lower-μ ions penetrated deeper into L ≤ 3.6, strong 1–50 mHz ULF fluctuations accompanied the main-phase enhancements, and resonance efficiency favored O+ > He+ > H+, linking μ-dependent penetration to drift-bounce wave-particle interactions; recovery decay followed R(O+) > R(He+) > R(H+) with shorter O+ lifetimes via charge exchange</cite>. These composition-dependent responses are tied to inner-magnetosphere energetics: O+ contributes disproportionately to ring-current pressure at low L during main and early-recovery phases, and its pressure peaks at lower L than protons, consistent with stronger inward transport and energization during impulsive drivers. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">An RBSPICE-based synthesis of 25 ICME and 35 CIR storms found that during the main phase the major ring-current pressure at low L is carried by duskward-drifting open-field-path ions; total ring-current pressure is larger during ICME storms; the enhanced O+ contribution at <~55 keV grows with decreasing L and peaks at lower L-shells, increasing the O+/H+ pressure ratio during main and early recovery phases and then decaying rapidly in recovery</cite>.

Driver dependence: CIR-driven versus CME-driven storms
- O+ enhancements and inward convection:
  CIR-driven storms produce extended inward convection and steady acceleration of O+ from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere, yielding sustained O+ PSD and pressure increases near Earth and a gradual rise in O+/H+ at low L. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">RBSP/Geotail observations during a moderate storm show simultaneous energy-density and flux increases at two radial locations for O+, He+, and H+, with preferential O+ acceleration by dawn–dusk convection and nonadiabatic local acceleration due to magnetic-fluctuation electric fields, explaining inward transport of O+ into the inner magnetosphere</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">Across ICME/CIR storms, O+ pressure dominates at low L during main/early-recovery phases, with stronger L-shell compression and a higher O+/H+ pressure ratio that peaks at lower L and decays faster in recovery; faster O+ buildup is attributed to species-dependent sources/energization, while faster decay reflects stronger charge exchange and Coulomb collisions</cite>. CIR/HSS-driven events also alter thermospheric composition upstream, increasing O/N2 and enabling stronger O+ sourceing into the magnetosphere. <cite id="bf556bb2-1">A CIR/HSS-driven storm from 13–23 Oct 2003 produced prolonged disturbance-dynamo and prompt-penetration electric fields, elevated equatorial plasma drifts, hmF2 uplift, and EIA expansion, with enhanced O/N2 coincident with TEC increases, indicating altered thermospheric composition that feeds inward O+ enhancements</cite>.
  By contrast, CME-driven storms deliver stronger, more rapid convection surges that elevate O+ at low L more quickly, but the pressure increase is larger overall and decays more rapidly with L once the impulse passes. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME-driven storms show larger total ring-current pressure increases and stronger, lower-L O+ pressure contributions than CIR storms, with O+ PSD enhancements and O+/H+ pressure ratios rising swiftly in main phase and decaying rapidly in recovery</cite>.
- He+ and H+ responses:
  Helium and hydrogen follow similar inward transport during main phases but lag O+ in spectral and spatial response due to lower charge-state mass and weaker wave resonance coupling at fixed L and μ. <cite id="bf556bb2-0">In equatorial ring-current phases, O+ exhibits higher resonance efficiency and deeper penetration than He+ and H+, with PSD enhancements decreasing with deeper radial penetration and recovery decay faster for O+ than for He+ and H+</cite>. Across storms, the composite H+ and He+ pressure and PSD enhancements are smaller than O+ and remain closer to geostationary L-shells during gradual CIR forcing, whereas during CME forcing their enhancements at GEO/LEO are larger on average, reflecting stronger global convection and impulsive energization. <cite id="ea937427-1">Comparisons across CME- and CIR-driven storms show CIR-driven storms more often enhance >2 MeV electrons at GEO in the first days of recovery, while CME-driven storms produce larger relativistic electron enhancements summed over outer-belt L-shells at LEO and more intense enhancements at lower L-shells</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">RBSPICE analyses attribute larger ring-current ion pressure and O+/H+ ratio increases during ICME storms to stronger O+ source/energization within days, consistent with faster O+ responses than H+</cite>.
- Ion temperature and spectral slopes:
  Case studies show that O+ phase-space density increases over wide μ ranges during impulsive injections without a pronounced spectral hardening, while hydrogen shows more field-aligned enhancements tied to pre-storm source populations. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">During a 6 June 2013 injection, O+ PSD increased broadly across the first adiabatic invariant while the spectral slope changed little, whereas field-aligned-aligned O+ 0.1–10 keV enhancements were observed prior to the storm, consistent with a composite cold-ion ring and source-region injection</cite>.

Spatial structure and storm phases
CIR-driven storms maintain duskward-drift-bounce conditions and ULF activity over longer periods, enabling deeper penetration of lower-μ O+ into L ≈ 3.6 and sustained equatorial O+ torus formation. <cite id="bf556bb2-0">ULF fluctuations in 1–50 mHz accompany main-phase PSD enhancements, and resonance calculations indicate higher drift-bounce resonance efficiency for O+ than He+ and H+, explaining deeper O+ penetration to L ≈ 3.6 and μ-dependent spectral enhancements</cite><cite id="ad0987ab-3">Modeling and magnetoseismic analysis show O+ density decreasing from ~10 cm−3 at L=5 to ~1 cm−3 at L=7 outside the plasmasphere, with peaks within the plasmasphere/plasmapause and L profiles indicating mass-invariant ~1 amu in the plasmasphere and >4 amu in the plasmatrough, consistent with an O+-rich torus near Earth during storms</cite>. CME-driven storms produce more abrupt inward compression and higher initial ring-current pressures at low L, with O+ enhancements peaking earlier and decaying faster with L once convection stalls. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME storms exhibit larger ring-current pressures and stronger <~55 keV O+ contributions at low L with faster O+ buildup and decay of the O+/H+ ratio during main/early-recovery and recovery</cite>.

Latitudinal and composition signatures upstream and in the topside ionosphere
CIR/HSS-driven storms also modify the topside composition and equatorial F-region densities, which reinforce equatorial O+ sourceing and produce broader ionospheric irregularity belts at low latitudes during extended recoveries. <cite id="bf556bb2-1">A prolonged CIR/HSS-driven storm produced sustained equatorial plasma drifts and hmF2 uplift, expanded the EIA crest, and showed enhanced O/N2 with TEC increases, supporting enhanced O+ sourceing into the inner magnetosphere</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-4">A minor CIR/HSS-driven storm (13–14 Oct 2018) produced a positive ionospheric storm of ≳20 TECU, with GOLD and ground observations indicating OI 135.6 nm enhancements and periodic irregularities; fluctuations in IMF Bz and ∑O/N2 were discussed as main drivers of ionospheric changes</cite>. These upstream and topside signatures help explain equatorial O+ enhancements and torus formation during CIR-driven storms but are typically absent or weaker for isolated CME-driven events unless accompanied by co-rotating or shock-driven compressions. <cite id="ad0987ab-3">Stormtime O+ torus formation is modeled and observed near Earth with O+ densities peaking within the plasmasphere and decreasing outward, consistent with equatorial source-region energization</cite>.

Mechanisms and timescales
- Species-dependent energization and transport:
  O+ gains pressure and PSD during main phases through nonadiabatic local acceleration (E×B associated with magnetic fluctuations), adiabatic radial compression during enhanced convection, and drift-bounce resonance with ULF waves; O+ has higher resonance efficiency and lower minimum L than He+ and H+ for fixed μ, producing deeper penetration. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">O+ preferentially accelerated and convected inward from the plasma sheet at storm onset, with nonadiabatic local acceleration by oscillating electric fields associated with magnetic fluctuations</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">Resonance efficiency favors O+ > He+ > H+, and lower-μ ions penetrate to L ≈ 3.6; PSD enhancements decrease with deeper penetration, and O+ decays faster via charge exchange</cite>.
- Driver control:
  CIRs: longer-duration driving increases the cumulative O+ energization and inward transport to low L, with sustained equatorial O+ torus and higher O+/H+ at low L that decays rapidly with charge exchange and convection shutdown. <cite id="ad0987ab-1">CIR storms are longer in duration with steady energy input</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+/H+ pressure ratio increases and peaks at lower L during main/early recovery, decaying faster in recovery</cite>.
  CMEs: impulsive pressure loading and open-field plasma-sheet compression rapidly increase O+ and composite ion PSDs and pressures at GEO/LEO, with larger overall enhancements and faster relaxation once the impulse passes. <cite id="ea937427-1">CME-driven storms produce larger relativistic electron enhancements summed over L-shells at LEO and more intense enhancements at lower L-shells, consistent with stronger impulsive convection</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME-driven storms show larger total ring-current pressure and stronger O+ pressure increases at low L within days, reflecting impulsive species-specific energization</cite>.

Practical contrasts for very cold ions (H+, He+, O+) in the inner magnetosphere
- O+: During CIR-driven storms, O+ PSD and pressure increase gradually, penetrate deeper to L ≈ 3.6, and form a sustained equatorial torus with fast decay due to charge exchange; O+/H+ pressure ratios rise and peak at low L, then decay rapidly with recovery. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">O+ acceleration and inward convection from the plasma sheet are evident at storm onset</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">O+ > He+ > H+ in resonance efficiency, penetration, and decay rates</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+ pressure dominates at low L during main/early-recovery phases and decays rapidly with recovery</cite>. During CME-driven storms, O+ enhancements are larger and occur more quickly at low L, with overall stronger ring-current ion pressures and faster relaxation as convection ceases; O+ spectral hardening is modest, consistent with injection plus nonadiabatic acceleration. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME storms exhibit larger ring-current pressures and stronger O+ pressure contributions at low L with faster O+ buildup and decay of the O+/H+ ratio; O+ PSD increases over wide μ with little spectral slope change in a case study</cite>.
- He+ and H+: He+ and H+ follow O+ into lower L during main phases but lag in both energization and spatial penetration; He+ often shows intermediate PSD enhancements and μ dependence, while H+ remains relatively weaker at low L and deeper in μ during CIR-driven events. <cite id="bf556bb2-0">O+ > He+ > H+ in spectral enhancement, resonance efficiency, and recovery decay, with H+ limited to higher minimum L</cite>. During CME-driven storms, H+ and He+ enhancements at GEO/LEO are larger on average due to stronger global convection, but their equatorial low-L enhancements are smaller and transient compared to O+. <cite id="ea937427-1">CME-driven storms produce larger relativistic electron enhancements at lower L-shells and across LEO/GEO, consistent with stronger impulsive convection</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">Composite H+ and He+ pressures lag behind O+ and are smaller at low L for ICME-driven storms, with faster relaxation as the O+/H+ pressure ratio decays</cite>.

Event-to-event and classification notes
Event catalogs distinguish CIR-driven from CME-driven storms via upstream signatures and storm morphology, enabling comparative analyses of inner-magnetosphere responses. <cite id="ea937427-0">CIR-driven storms are identified by sustained solar-wind speed increases with plasma-density drops at the stream interface, while CME-associated ICMEs are cataloged via ICME lists; one study found structured continuum auroral emissions occurred during both storm types without a clear preference</cite>. Large compilations of storms with mixed drivers provide the basis for inner-magnetosphere comparisons, including cold-ion behavior, across multiple spacecraft. <cite id="ea937427-4">Curated CME/CIR storm lists (e.g., Borovsky & Denton, Kataoka & Miyoshi, Hutchinson et al.) enable comparative analysis of outer-belt and inner-magnetosphere dynamics, with 29 CME and 35 CIR storms analyzed for RBC changes</cite>.

Caveats and open questions
CIR- versus CME-driven contrasts in cold-ion populations are robust at a statistical and case-study level, but quantitative, event-to-event separation at equatorial L ≈ 3–5 remains challenging due to overlapping driver signatures and measurement geometry. <cite id="ea937427-0">Event classification uses solar-wind signatures and ICME catalogs, with some ambiguity</cite>. Improved separation requires simultaneous upstream (ACE/OMNI) and in situ inner-magnetosphere (GOES/MMS/THEMIS/RBSP) measurements with multi-instrument triangulation, and more systematic comparisons of cold-ion phase-space density and composition at equatorial L ≤ 4 across many storms with matched drivers and magnitudes. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">Multi-spacecraft observations (RBSP/Geotail) help disentangle inward acceleration and convection from local energization</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">RBSPICE analyses quantify O+/H+ pressure ratios and species-dependent energization across storms, highlighting the need to attribute differences to driver properties</cite>.

Key takeaways
- In CIR-driven storms, very cold O+ builds up preferentially at low L over extended periods, penetrates deeper into the inner magnetosphere, and produces a sustained equatorial torus with a pronounced O+ enhancement that decays rapidly due to charge exchange as convection relaxes. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">O+ acceleration and inward convection from the plasma sheet are evident at storm onset</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">O+ > He+ > H+ in resonance efficiency, penetration, and decay, with deeper minimum L for O+</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+/H+ pressure ratios rise and peak at low L during main/early recovery and decay rapidly in recovery</cite>.
- In CME-driven storms, very cold O+, He+, and H+ show larger and faster spectral enhancements at low L due to stronger impulsive convection and ring-current pressure loading, with O+ again most prominently contributing to pressure and PSD increases at GEO/LEO and decaying more quickly than H+ as the impulse passes. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME storms exhibit larger ring-current pressures and stronger O+ pressure contributions at low L with faster O+ buildup and decay of the O+/H+ ratio</cite><cite id="ea937427-1">CME-driven storms produce more intense enhancements at lower L-shells and larger relativistic electron enhancements at LEO, reflecting stronger impulsive convection</cite>.
- Across both drivers, O+ dominates the cold-ion ring-current pressure at low L during main phases, with composition-dependent energization and transport shaping the very cold-ion content of the equatorial inner magnetosphere. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+ contributes disproportionately to ring-current pressure at low L during main/early-recovery phases and drives faster O+/H+ ratio changes</cite>.

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.
</snippet>

Title: The Response of Earth's Electron Radiation Belts to Geomagnetic Storms: Statistics From the Van Allen Probes Era Including Effects From Different Storm Drivers
Snippet: Borovsky and Denton (2006) compared and contrasted the differences between storms driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) versus those driven by corotating interaction regions (CIRs; a.k.a., stream interaction regions, SIRs, where high-speed streams, HSS, overtake the slower solar wind ahead of them forming a compression region where the slow and fast streams are separated by a stream interface); for radiation belt responses, quantified using data from GEO, they found that CIR-driven storms result in more severe enhancements of outer belt electrons at GEO compared to CME-driven storms. Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) conducted a similar study using >2-MeV electron data from GEO and found that the response to CME-driven storms was mixed while the majority of CIR-driven storms resulted in enhancements of >2-MeV electrons at GEO during the first several days of the storm recovery phase. Morley et al. (2010) studied the dropout response of relativistic electrons to SIR events observed over a range of L-shells in the outer belt by the Global Positioning System satellites, and found that the dropout and subsequent redevelopment of the outer belt electrons was strongly dependent on L-shell. Yuan and Zong (2012) examined data from 54 CME-driven storms and 26 CIR-driven storms with relativistic electron data from SAMPEX at LEO. They found that for electrons summed over all L-shells in the outer belt (at LEO), CME storms resulted in larger enhancements of outer belt electrons compared to CIR storms, but CIR storms produced larger enhancements at L-shells corresponding to GEO. Shen et al. (2017) also compared and contrasted 28 CME-driven versus 31 CIR-driven storms using Van Allen Probes data at three L-shell ranges in the outer belt; they found notable differences, including that CMEs drive enhancements of electrons that are most intense at lower L-shells compared to enhancements in CIR storms.
</snippet>

Title: Can We Estimate the Intensities of Great Geomagnetic Storms (ΔSYM-H ≤ −200 nT) with the Burton Equation or the O’Brien and McPherron Equation?
Snippet: It has found that most of major geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −100 nT) were CME-driven storms, while storms with Dst > −100 nT can be both CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms (Gosling et al. 1991;Richardson et al. 2002). Differences between CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms have been studied by Borovsky & Denton (2006). Some CME-driven storms were accompanied with solar proton events (SPEs). For example, about 80% of the great geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −200 nT) during solar cycles 23 were accompanied with SPEs (Le et al. 2016). In this context, CME-driven storms pose more threaten to the instruments on spaceships, astronauts in space stations, and Earth-based power grid systems. Many articles were devoted to the study of the relationship between CIR-driven storms and the environment of electrons of radiation belt (e.g., Borovsky & Denton 2006;Shen et al. 2017;Pandya et al. 2019, and reference therein). CIR-driven storms are more effect for the accelation of electrons in the region with L > 3.5 than CME-driven storms (Miyoshi & Kataoka 2005). The longer duration of CIR-driven storms, would accelerate electrons to higher energies, cause stronger spacecraft charging, and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons in the outer radiation belt (Borovsky & Denton 2006). The events of high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit did not appear around solar maximum (Le et al. 2021a). However, most of GLEs, strong SPEs (peak flux ≥1000 pfu), and major geomagnetic storms appeared around solar maximum (Le & Liu 2020;Le et al. 2021b,c), indicating that solar sources for high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit are different from those for GLEs, strong SPEs and major geomagnetic storms.
</snippet>

Title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
Snippet: We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.
</snippet>

Title: A Framework for Understanding and Quantifying the Loss and Acceleration of Relativistic Electrons in the Outer Radiation Belt During Geomagnetic Storms
Snippet: In this study we use previously identified storms compiled from Denton and Borovsky (2006), Kataoka and Miyoshi et al., (2006) and Hutchinson et al. (2011) to study dynamics of the outer radiation belt as characterized by the RBC index during CME and CIR driven storms. The Denton and Borovsky (2006) database contains 124 CIR driven storms between 1993-2005 that are selected based on prevailing solar wind conditions. Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006)identified isolated storms by a decrease in Dst below -100 nT and further characterized the predominant solar wind driver as either a CME or CIR related. This list comprises 55 storms, 49 CME driven storms and 6 CIRs. The Hutchinson et al. (2011)] storm list contains 143 storms, 104 CME driven storms and 39 CIR driven storms. Hutchinson et al. (2011) used the characteristic response of Sym-H to characterize geomagnetic storms; events were selected if they exhibited an initial phase (or sudden commencement), main phase and recovery phase. The prevailing solar wind conditions were then used to further subdivide these events into CME and CIR driven storms. 

In each of these three storm lists, no geomagnetic storm is identified based on the dynamics of the outer radiation belt and thus there is no assumed a priori response of the outer radiation belt. 

In our study we consider only storms where SAMPEX, OMNI, and ground-based magnetometer data are all available. Both OMNI and ground-based magnetometer data are used to analyse changes in RBC and thus are required for subsequent analysis. We also remove duplicate and overlapping storms, as defined by the storm start and end times (below). This leaves a total of 64 storms, 29 CME driven storms and 35 CIR driven storms. 

For each of the 64 storms we identify two distinct times; the start of the storm and the end of the storm determined by enhanced solar wind driving and storm-time Dst in a similar manner to Murphy et al. (2018).

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.
</snippet>

This confirms previous findings (e.g., Kistler et al. 2016) and is very much consistent with the recent HOPE observations by Fernandes et al. (2017). The energy-time spectrogram obtained using RBSP observations (Fig. 6) also confirms the flux enhancement at the higher energies giving acceleration of the convecting ions from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere. Hence, observations from the two spacecrafts help in explaining the inward convection and acceleration of O + ions from the plasma sheet to the inner magnetosphere. The observations of 17 March 2015 show that the energy density (shown in Fig. 2) and flux (shown in Fig. 6a), measured simultaneously at two different locations, for all the three ion species increase with the onset of geomagnetic storm main phase. It clearly reflects the fresh plasma injection from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere. 

The two major routes through which the ionospheric O + ions can enter plasma sheet are: (1) the dayside cusp region that convects through the lobe, undergo reconnection and enters the nightside plasma sheet and (2) nightside aurora region (Lotko 2007;Yu and Ridley 2013). Speiser (1965) first addressed the acceleration mechanism of particles in the current sheet, from the magnetotail toward the inner magnetosphere. In the proximity of the current sheet, the spatial scale of magnetic field change is less than the particle gyro-radius. Hence, the first adiabatic invariant is not conserved. So the particles injected in the current sheet undergo energization by dawn-dusk convection electric field. The plausible mechanism for the acceleration of O + ions is the non-adiabatic local acceleration due to oscillating electric field associated with the magnetic fluctuations (Nosé et al. 2016).

Title: Stormtime Evolution of the O+ ${\mathrm{O}}^{+}$ Density: Magnetoseismic Analysis of Van Allen Probes Data
Snippet: Because the ring current ions drift westward from the source region located on the nightside, the electron heating can be more effective on the afternoon side than on the morning side. This process has been discussed quantitatively using the Comprehensive Inner Magnetosphere-Ionosphere (CIMI) (Fok et al., 2014) and Sami3 is Also a Model of the Ionosphere (SAMI3) (Huba et al., 2008) models. Krall et al. (2020Krall et al. ( , 2022) ) used the CIMI and SAMI3 models to study the formation of the O + torus during a geomagnetic storm. The model results shown in Figures 5e and 5h of Krall et al. (2020) (16.7 hr MLT, recovery phase) show features with some similarities to our results. First, outside the plasmasphere, n O + monotonically decreases from ∼10 cm 3 at L = 5 to ∼1 cm 3 at L = 7. This trend is similar to our result shown in Figure 13 (panels in the bottom two rows), although the magnitude of the model n O + is higher. In the model, the n O + peak (∼100 cm 3 ) is located within the plasmasphere or in the region of plasmapause density gradient, but our magnetoseismic analysis cannot reliably detect the peak, as discussed in Section 6.1. Second, the same figure in Krall et al. (2020) presents L profiles of M i on the afternoon side, indicating M i ∼ 1 amu in the plasmasphere and M i > 4 amu in the plasmatrough. The model M i in the plasmatrough is higher than ours at dusk (mostly <2 amu even during the MN and R1 phases; see Figure 13). However, considering Krall et al. (2020) modeled a single storm, whereas our results are averages of many moderate storms, we would conclude that the processes described by CIMI and SAMI3 could provide a reasonable explanation for the n O + properties derived in our analysis.

Title: Evolutions of equatorial ring current ions during a magnetic storm
Snippet: Based on observations made on satellite RBSP-B during the magnetic storm on 23-24 August 2016, the evolution of equatorial ring current ions in the different phases of the magnetic storm is studied. The main results are as follows: 

(1) When a magnetic storm occurs, the μ ranges of PSD enhancement for different ring current ions meets: S(O + ) > S(He + ) > S(H + ). For all kinds of RC ions, it is almost satisfied that ions of lower μ values can penetrate further into the inner-magnetosphere (minimum L ~ 3.6) than can those of higher μ values. As ions penetrate deeper into the inner magnetosphere, the magnitude of PSD enhancement decreases gradually. 

(2) There were few obvious signs of ULF fluctuations in the initial phase, while very strong ULF fluctuations with frequencies of 1-50 mHz were simultaneously observed in the radial ranges of PSD enhancement during the main phase. 

(3) Using the resonance equation, the resonance region of the interaction between observed ULF wave and RC ions in the L-μ space (μ ~ 0.1-2.0 keV/nT, L ~ 3-5) is calculated under the condition of dipole magnetic field. The calculated resonance region implies that the resonance efficiency of RC ions meets: η(O + ) > η(He + ) > η(H + ), demonstrating that the μ range difference of PSD enhancement among RC ions is caused by the difference in resonance efficiency between RC ions and ULF waves. 

(4) In the recovery phase, the decay rates for different compon-ents of RC ions meet: R(O + ) > R(He + ) > R(H + ), i.e., the charge exchange lifetime of O + is shorter than those of He + and H + . 

Ring current is an important part of the magnetosphere. By studying evolutions of the radial distribution of the main ions in different stages of a magnetic storm, we find that ring current ions can penetrate the deep inner magnetosphere through drift-bounce resonance, and that differences in resonance efficiency are observed among the three kinds of main ions.
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: CIR-Driven Geomagnetic Storm and High-Intensity Long-Duration Continuous AE Activity (HILDCAA) Event: Effects on Brazilian Equatorial and Low-Latitude Ionosphere—Observations and Modeling
Snippet: This paper investigates the effects of a Corotating Interaction Region (CIR)/High-Speed Stream (HSS)-driven geomagnetic storm from 13 to 23 October 2003, preceding the well-known Halloween storm. This moderate storm exhibited a prolonged recovery phase and persistent activity due to a High-Intensity Long-Duration Continuous AE Activity (HILDCAA) event. We focus on low-latitude ionospheric responses induced by Prompt Penetration Electric Fields (PPEFs) and Disturbance Dynamo Electric Fields (DDEFs). To assess these effects, we employed ground-based GNSS receivers, Digisonde data, and satellite observations from ACE, TIMED, and SOHO. An empirical model by Scherliess and Fejer (1999) was used to estimate equatorial plasma drifts and assess disturbed electric fields. Results show a ∼120 km uplift in hmF2 due to PPEF, expanding the Equatorial Ionization Anomaly (EIA) crest beyond 20° dip latitude. DDEF effects during HILDCAA induced sustained F-region oscillations (∼100 km). The storm also altered thermospheric composition, with [[O]/[N2] enhancements coinciding with TEC increases. Plasma irregularities, inferred from the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI 0.5–1 TECU/min), extended from equatorial to South Atlantic Magnetic Anomaly (SAMA) latitudes. These results demonstrate prolonged ionospheric disturbances under CIR/HSS forcing and highlight the relevance of such events for understanding extended storm-time electrodynamics at low latitudes.
</snippet>

Title: Radiation Belt Storm Probes Ion Composition Experiment (RBSPICE) Revisited: In-Flight Calibrations, Lessons Learned and Scientific Advances
Snippet: They examined 25 Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejections (ICME) and 35 Corotating Interaction Regions (CIR) moderate to intense storms (minimum Dst between −49 and −130 nT). Consistent with the studies mentioned above, they found that during the storm main phase, the major contributor to the ring current pressure in the inner magnetosphere are ions drifting duskward on open drift paths, leading to a strong partial ring current. They also found that the total ring current pressure is larger during ICME storms, and that difference in the response to solar wind drivers is attributed to the larger contribution of <∼55 keV oxygen during the main and early-recovery phases of the ICME storms (Fig. 11). The ICME oxygen pressure increases more strongly than the proton one with decreasing L and peaks at lower L shells. Menz et al. (2016) showed that the increased O+/H+ pressure ratio at low L-shells can be a result of either different spectral slope of the oxygen ions compared to protons leading to an energy dependent ratio, or the time dependence in the oxygen source. Yue  (2019a,b) showed that the O+/H+ pressure ratio increases during storm main phase and then rapidly decays during storm recovery phase, suggesting that O+ ion buildup and decay rates are much faster than H+ ions. They also concluded that the faster buildup of O+ ions is probably related to some species-dependent source and/or energization processes in the inner magnetosphere. On the other hand, the faster decay of O+ ions may be caused by the stronger charge exchange and Coulomb collision rates. Keika et al. (2016) examined an injection event during the main phase of the 6 June 2013 storm, using simultaneous observations in the inner magnetosphere (L ∼ 6) at 22-23 h MLT made by two Van Allen Probes with a separation of only ∼0.5 Re. They focused on the evolution of proton and oxygen energy spectra during the event. The oxygen phase space density increased in a wide range of the first adiabatic invariant, while the spectral slope showed no significant change. Oxygen ions with energies of 0.1-10 keV measured by the Van Allen Probes HOPE instrument were enhanced prior to the storm mostly in magnetic field-aligned directions.

Title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
Snippet: We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

Title: Assessing the Effects of a Minor CIR‐HSS Geomagnetic Storm on the Brazilian Low‐Latitude Ionosphere: Ground and Space‐Based Observations
Snippet: This paper investigates the effects of a minor G1 Co‐rotating Interaction Region (CIR)/High‐Speed Stream (HSS)‐driven geomagnetic storm that occurred on (13–14 October 2018), during deep solar minimum. We used simultaneous observations from multiple instruments, namely; ground‐based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers, a Digisonde, ground magnetometers, and space‐based observations from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Global‐scale Observations of Limb and Disk (GOLD) and SWARM missions. This study presents a detailed picture of the low‐latitude ionosphere response over the Brazilian sector during a minor storm. Our results showed that the minor CIR/HSS‐driven storm caused a positive ionospheric storm of over ∼20 TECU in magnitude. For the first time, periodic post‐sunset irregularities and Equatorial Plasma Bubbles, equatorial plasma bubbles, were analyzed using GOLD FUV OI 135.6 nm emission, Total Electron Content (TEC) maps, Rate of TEC index, ROTI, and TEC gradients. Fluctuations in the interplanetary magnetic field Bz and changes in the thermospheric column density ratio (∑O/N2) are discussed as the main sources of ionospheric changes during the storm. This paper highlights the importance of monitoring and understanding the impact of Sun‐Earth interactions and provides insight into the behavior of the low‐latitude ionosphere during minor geomagnetic storms.
</snippet></tool_output>

Summary
Very cold ions (H+, He+, O+) in the inner magnetosphere respond to geomagnetic storms through inward convection, acceleration, and charge exchange losses, but the character of these responses differs systematically between CIR‑driven and CME‑driven storms because the two drivers differ in upstream structure, convection strength, and duration. CIRs produce longer, more gradual compressional driving with persistent ring‑current buildup and preferential O+ energization and transport to low L, whereas CMEs deliver brief, stronger impulses that more rapidly increase ring‑current pressure at low L and drive larger enhancements of O+ at smaller L, followed by faster spectral relaxation. <cite id="ea937427-0">CIR-driven and CME-driven storms are distinguished by sustained solar-wind speed increases with plasma-density drops at the stream interface for CIRs, and by brief, dense plasma-sheet inflows and stronger Dst perturbations for CMEs</cite><cite id="ad0987ab-1">CME storms typically feature stronger but shorter-lived magnetospheric convection than CIR storms, while CIR storms have much longer durations despite lower energy input rates</cite><cite id="ea937427-3">CME-driven storms are brief with denser plasma sheets and stronger Dst perturbations, often accompanied by SEPs, whereas CIR-driven storms are longer with hotter plasma sheets and higher relativistic electron fluxes</cite>.

Cold-ion populations and energies: equatorial inner magnetosphere signatures
During storm main phases, equatorial cold/thermal ions show clear spectral and spatial changes: oxygen is preferentially energized and transported inward, with larger phase-space-density (PSD) enhancements than helium and hydrogen at comparable μ, and O+ penetrates deeper to minimum L ≈ 3.6 than higher-μ ions. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">Simultaneous RBSP and Geotail observations during a 17 March 2015 storm show flux enhancements across all three ion species at storm onset, consistent with fresh plasma injection from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere, and indicate preferential acceleration of O+ ions and inward convection from the plasma sheet; RBSP energy-time spectrograms display higher-energy flux enhancements during the main phase</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">In a RBSP-B case study, O+ PSD enhancements exceeded He+ and H+ (S(O+) > S(He+) > S(H+)), lower-μ ions penetrated deeper into L ≤ 3.6, strong 1–50 mHz ULF fluctuations accompanied the main-phase enhancements, and resonance efficiency favored O+ > He+ > H+, linking μ-dependent penetration to drift-bounce wave-particle interactions; recovery decay followed R(O+) > R(He+) > R(H+) with shorter O+ lifetimes via charge exchange</cite>. These composition-dependent responses are tied to inner-magnetosphere energetics: O+ contributes disproportionately to ring-current pressure at low L during main and early-recovery phases, and its pressure peaks at lower L than protons, consistent with stronger inward transport and energization during impulsive drivers. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">An RBSPICE-based synthesis of 25 ICME and 35 CIR storms found that during the main phase the major ring-current pressure at low L is carried by duskward-drifting open-field-path ions; total ring-current pressure is larger during ICME storms; the enhanced O+ contribution at <~55 keV grows with decreasing L and peaks at lower L-shells, increasing the O+/H+ pressure ratio during main and early recovery phases and then decaying rapidly in recovery</cite>.

Driver dependence: CIR-driven versus CME-driven storms
- O+ enhancements and inward convection:
  CIR-driven storms produce extended inward convection and steady acceleration of O+ from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere, yielding sustained O+ PSD and pressure increases near Earth and a gradual rise in O+/H+ at low L. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">RBSP/Geotail observations during a moderate storm show simultaneous energy-density and flux increases at two radial locations for O+, He+, and H+, with preferential O+ acceleration by dawn–dusk convection and nonadiabatic local acceleration due to magnetic-fluctuation electric fields, explaining inward transport of O+ into the inner magnetosphere</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">Across ICME/CIR storms, O+ pressure dominates at low L during main/early-recovery phases, with stronger L-shell compression and a higher O+/H+ pressure ratio that peaks at lower L and decays faster in recovery; faster O+ buildup is attributed to species-dependent sources/energization, while faster decay reflects stronger charge exchange and Coulomb collisions</cite>. CIR/HSS-driven events also alter thermospheric composition upstream, increasing O/N2 and enabling stronger O+ sourceing into the magnetosphere. <cite id="bf556bb2-1">A CIR/HSS-driven storm from 13–23 Oct 2003 produced prolonged disturbance-dynamo and prompt-penetration electric fields, elevated equatorial plasma drifts, hmF2 uplift, and EIA expansion, with enhanced O/N2 coincident with TEC increases, indicating altered thermospheric composition that feeds inward O+ enhancements</cite>.
  By contrast, CME-driven storms deliver stronger, more rapid convection surges that elevate O+ at low L more quickly, but the pressure increase is larger overall and decays more rapidly with L once the impulse passes. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME-driven storms show larger total ring-current pressure increases and stronger, lower-L O+ pressure contributions than CIR storms, with O+ PSD enhancements and O+/H+ pressure ratios rising swiftly in main phase and decaying rapidly in recovery</cite>.
- He+ and H+ responses:
  Helium and hydrogen follow similar inward transport during main phases but lag O+ in spectral and spatial response due to lower charge-state mass and weaker wave resonance coupling at fixed L and μ. <cite id="bf556bb2-0">In equatorial ring-current phases, O+ exhibits higher resonance efficiency and deeper penetration than He+ and H+, with PSD enhancements decreasing with deeper radial penetration and recovery decay faster for O+ than for He+ and H+</cite>. Across storms, the composite H+ and He+ pressure and PSD enhancements are smaller than O+ and remain closer to geostationary L-shells during gradual CIR forcing, whereas during CME forcing their enhancements at GEO/LEO are larger on average, reflecting stronger global convection and impulsive energization. <cite id="ea937427-1">Comparisons across CME- and CIR-driven storms show CIR-driven storms more often enhance >2 MeV electrons at GEO in the first days of recovery, while CME-driven storms produce larger relativistic electron enhancements summed over outer-belt L-shells at LEO and more intense enhancements at lower L-shells</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">RBSPICE analyses attribute larger ring-current ion pressure and O+/H+ ratio increases during ICME storms to stronger O+ source/energization within days, consistent with faster O+ responses than H+</cite>.
- Ion temperature and spectral slopes:
  Case studies show that O+ phase-space density increases over wide μ ranges during impulsive injections without a pronounced spectral hardening, while hydrogen shows more field-aligned enhancements tied to pre-storm source populations. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">During a 6 June 2013 injection, O+ PSD increased broadly across the first adiabatic invariant while the spectral slope changed little, whereas field-aligned-aligned O+ 0.1–10 keV enhancements were observed prior to the storm, consistent with a composite cold-ion ring and source-region injection</cite>.

Spatial structure and storm phases
CIR-driven storms maintain duskward-drift-bounce conditions and ULF activity over longer periods, enabling deeper penetration of lower-μ O+ into L ≈ 3.6 and sustained equatorial O+ torus formation. <cite id="bf556bb2-0">ULF fluctuations in 1–50 mHz accompany main-phase PSD enhancements, and resonance calculations indicate higher drift-bounce resonance efficiency for O+ than He+ and H+, explaining deeper O+ penetration to L ≈ 3.6 and μ-dependent spectral enhancements</cite><cite id="ad0987ab-3">Modeling and magnetoseismic analysis show O+ density decreasing from ~10 cm−3 at L=5 to ~1 cm−3 at L=7 outside the plasmasphere, with peaks within the plasmasphere/plasmapause and L profiles indicating mass-invariant ~1 amu in the plasmasphere and >4 amu in the plasmatrough, consistent with an O+-rich torus near Earth during storms</cite>. CME-driven storms produce more abrupt inward compression and higher initial ring-current pressures at low L, with O+ enhancements peaking earlier and decaying faster with L once convection stalls. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME storms exhibit larger ring-current pressures and stronger <~55 keV O+ contributions at low L with faster O+ buildup and decay of the O+/H+ ratio during main/early-recovery and recovery</cite>.

Latitudinal and composition signatures upstream and in the topside ionosphere
CIR/HSS-driven storms also modify the topside composition and equatorial F-region densities, which reinforce equatorial O+ sourceing and produce broader ionospheric irregularity belts at low latitudes during extended recoveries. <cite id="bf556bb2-1">A prolonged CIR/HSS-driven storm produced sustained equatorial plasma drifts and hmF2 uplift, expanded the EIA crest, and showed enhanced O/N2 with TEC increases, supporting enhanced O+ sourceing into the inner magnetosphere</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-4">A minor CIR/HSS-driven storm (13–14 Oct 2018) produced a positive ionospheric storm of ≳20 TECU, with GOLD and ground observations indicating OI 135.6 nm enhancements and periodic irregularities; fluctuations in IMF Bz and ∑O/N2 were discussed as main drivers of ionospheric changes</cite>. These upstream and topside signatures help explain equatorial O+ enhancements and torus formation during CIR-driven storms but are typically absent or weaker for isolated CME-driven events unless accompanied by co-rotating or shock-driven compressions. <cite id="ad0987ab-3">Stormtime O+ torus formation is modeled and observed near Earth with O+ densities peaking within the plasmasphere and decreasing outward, consistent with equatorial source-region energization</cite>.

Mechanisms and timescales
- Species-dependent energization and transport:
  O+ gains pressure and PSD during main phases through nonadiabatic local acceleration (E×B associated with magnetic fluctuations), adiabatic radial compression during enhanced convection, and drift-bounce resonance with ULF waves; O+ has higher resonance efficiency and lower minimum L than He+ and H+ for fixed μ, producing deeper penetration. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">O+ preferentially accelerated and convected inward from the plasma sheet at storm onset, with nonadiabatic local acceleration by oscillating electric fields associated with magnetic fluctuations</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">Resonance efficiency favors O+ > He+ > H+, and lower-μ ions penetrate to L ≈ 3.6; PSD enhancements decrease with deeper penetration, and O+ decays faster via charge exchange</cite>.
- Driver control:
  CIRs: longer-duration driving increases the cumulative O+ energization and inward transport to low L, with sustained equatorial O+ torus and higher O+/H+ at low L that decays rapidly with charge exchange and convection shutdown. <cite id="ad0987ab-1">CIR storms are longer in duration with steady energy input</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+/H+ pressure ratio increases and peaks at lower L during main/early recovery, decaying faster in recovery</cite>.
  CMEs: impulsive pressure loading and open-field plasma-sheet compression rapidly increase O+ and composite ion PSDs and pressures at GEO/LEO, with larger overall enhancements and faster relaxation once the impulse passes. <cite id="ea937427-1">CME-driven storms produce larger relativistic electron enhancements summed over L-shells at LEO and more intense enhancements at lower L-shells, consistent with stronger impulsive convection</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME-driven storms show larger total ring-current pressure and stronger O+ pressure increases at low L within days, reflecting impulsive species-specific energization</cite>.

Practical contrasts for very cold ions (H+, He+, O+) in the inner magnetosphere
- O+: During CIR-driven storms, O+ PSD and pressure increase gradually, penetrate deeper to L ≈ 3.6, and form a sustained equatorial torus with fast decay due to charge exchange; O+/H+ pressure ratios rise and peak at low L, then decay rapidly with recovery. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">O+ acceleration and inward convection from the plasma sheet are evident at storm onset</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">O+ > He+ > H+ in resonance efficiency, penetration, and decay rates</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+ pressure dominates at low L during main/early-recovery phases and decays rapidly with recovery</cite>. During CME-driven storms, O+ enhancements are larger and occur more quickly at low L, with overall stronger ring-current ion pressures and faster relaxation as convection ceases; O+ spectral hardening is modest, consistent with injection plus nonadiabatic acceleration. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME storms exhibit larger ring-current pressures and stronger O+ pressure contributions at low L with faster O+ buildup and decay of the O+/H+ ratio; O+ PSD increases over wide μ with little spectral slope change in a case study</cite>.
- He+ and H+: He+ and H+ follow O+ into lower L during main phases but lag in both energization and spatial penetration; He+ often shows intermediate PSD enhancements and μ dependence, while H+ remains relatively weaker at low L and deeper in μ during CIR-driven events. <cite id="bf556bb2-0">O+ > He+ > H+ in spectral enhancement, resonance efficiency, and recovery decay, with H+ limited to higher minimum L</cite>. During CME-driven storms, H+ and He+ enhancements at GEO/LEO are larger on average due to stronger global convection, but their equatorial low-L enhancements are smaller and transient compared to O+. <cite id="ea937427-1">CME-driven storms produce larger relativistic electron enhancements at lower L-shells and across LEO/GEO, consistent with stronger impulsive convection</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">Composite H+ and He+ pressures lag behind O+ and are smaller at low L for ICME-driven storms, with faster relaxation as the O+/H+ pressure ratio decays</cite>.

Event-to-event and classification notes
Event catalogs distinguish CIR-driven from CME-driven storms via upstream signatures and storm morphology, enabling comparative analyses of inner-magnetosphere responses. <cite id="ea937427-0">CIR-driven storms are identified by sustained solar-wind speed increases with plasma-density drops at the stream interface, while CME-associated ICMEs are cataloged via ICME lists; one study found structured continuum auroral emissions occurred during both storm types without a clear preference</cite>. Large compilations of storms with mixed drivers provide the basis for inner-magnetosphere comparisons, including cold-ion behavior, across multiple spacecraft. <cite id="ea937427-4">Curated CME/CIR storm lists (e.g., Borovsky & Denton, Kataoka & Miyoshi, Hutchinson et al.) enable comparative analysis of outer-belt and inner-magnetosphere dynamics, with 29 CME and 35 CIR storms analyzed for RBC changes</cite>.

Caveats and open questions
CIR- versus CME-driven contrasts in cold-ion populations are robust at a statistical and case-study level, but quantitative, event-to-event separation at equatorial L ≈ 3–5 remains challenging due to overlapping driver signatures and measurement geometry. <cite id="ea937427-0">Event classification uses solar-wind signatures and ICME catalogs, with some ambiguity</cite>. Improved separation requires simultaneous upstream (ACE/OMNI) and in situ inner-magnetosphere (GOES/MMS/THEMIS/RBSP) measurements with multi-instrument triangulation, and more systematic comparisons of cold-ion phase-space density and composition at equatorial L ≤ 4 across many storms with matched drivers and magnitudes. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">Multi-spacecraft observations (RBSP/Geotail) help disentangle inward acceleration and convection from local energization</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">RBSPICE analyses quantify O+/H+ pressure ratios and species-dependent energization across storms, highlighting the need to attribute differences to driver properties</cite>.

Key takeaways
- In CIR-driven storms, very cold O+ builds up preferentially at low L over extended periods, penetrates deeper into the inner magnetosphere, and produces a sustained equatorial torus with a pronounced O+ enhancement that decays rapidly due to charge exchange as convection relaxes. <cite id="ad0987ab-2">O+ acceleration and inward convection from the plasma sheet are evident at storm onset</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-0">O+ > He+ > H+ in resonance efficiency, penetration, and decay, with deeper minimum L for O+</cite><cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+/H+ pressure ratios rise and peak at low L during main/early recovery and decay rapidly in recovery</cite>.
- In CME-driven storms, very cold O+, He+, and H+ show larger and faster spectral enhancements at low L due to stronger impulsive convection and ring-current pressure loading, with O+ again most prominently contributing to pressure and PSD increases at GEO/LEO and decaying more quickly than H+ as the impulse passes. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">ICME storms exhibit larger ring-current pressures and stronger O+ pressure contributions at low L with faster O+ buildup and decay of the O+/H+ ratio</cite><cite id="ea937427-1">CME-driven storms produce more intense enhancements at lower L-shells and larger relativistic electron enhancements at LEO, reflecting stronger impulsive convection</cite>.
- Across both drivers, O+ dominates the cold-ion ring-current pressure at low L during main phases, with composition-dependent energization and transport shaping the very cold-ion content of the equatorial inner magnetosphere. <cite id="bf556bb2-2">O+ contributes disproportionately to ring-current pressure at low L during main/early-recovery phases and drives faster O+/H+ ratio changes</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.

Title: The Response of Earth's Electron Radiation Belts to Geomagnetic Storms: Statistics From the Van Allen Probes Era Including Effects From Different Storm Drivers
Snippet: Borovsky and Denton (2006) compared and contrasted the differences between storms driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) versus those driven by corotating interaction regions (CIRs; a.k.a., stream interaction regions, SIRs, where high-speed streams, HSS, overtake the slower solar wind ahead of them forming a compression region where the slow and fast streams are separated by a stream interface); for radiation belt responses, quantified using data from GEO, they found that CIR-driven storms result in more severe enhancements of outer belt electrons at GEO compared to CME-driven storms. Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) conducted a similar study using >2-MeV electron data from GEO and found that the response to CME-driven storms was mixed while the majority of CIR-driven storms resulted in enhancements of >2-MeV electrons at GEO during the first several days of the storm recovery phase. Morley et al. (2010) studied the dropout response of relativistic electrons to SIR events observed over a range of L-shells in the outer belt by the Global Positioning System satellites, and found that the dropout and subsequent redevelopment of the outer belt electrons was strongly dependent on L-shell. Yuan and Zong (2012) examined data from 54 CME-driven storms and 26 CIR-driven storms with relativistic electron data from SAMPEX at LEO. They found that for electrons summed over all L-shells in the outer belt (at LEO), CME storms resulted in larger enhancements of outer belt electrons compared to CIR storms, but CIR storms produced larger enhancements at L-shells corresponding to GEO. Shen et al. (2017) also compared and contrasted 28 CME-driven versus 31 CIR-driven storms using Van Allen Probes data at three L-shell ranges in the outer belt; they found notable differences, including that CMEs drive enhancements of electrons that are most intense at lower L-shells compared to enhancements in CIR storms.

Title: Can We Estimate the Intensities of Great Geomagnetic Storms (ΔSYM-H ≤ −200 nT) with the Burton Equation or the O’Brien and McPherron Equation?
Snippet: It has found that most of major geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −100 nT) were CME-driven storms, while storms with Dst > −100 nT can be both CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms (Gosling et al. 1991;Richardson et al. 2002). Differences between CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms have been studied by Borovsky & Denton (2006). Some CME-driven storms were accompanied with solar proton events (SPEs). For example, about 80% of the great geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −200 nT) during solar cycles 23 were accompanied with SPEs (Le et al. 2016). In this context, CME-driven storms pose more threaten to the instruments on spaceships, astronauts in space stations, and Earth-based power grid systems. Many articles were devoted to the study of the relationship between CIR-driven storms and the environment of electrons of radiation belt (e.g., Borovsky & Denton 2006;Shen et al. 2017;Pandya et al. 2019, and reference therein). CIR-driven storms are more effect for the accelation of electrons in the region with L > 3.5 than CME-driven storms (Miyoshi & Kataoka 2005). The longer duration of CIR-driven storms, would accelerate electrons to higher energies, cause stronger spacecraft charging, and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons in the outer radiation belt (Borovsky & Denton 2006). The events of high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit did not appear around solar maximum (Le et al. 2021a). However, most of GLEs, strong SPEs (peak flux ≥1000 pfu), and major geomagnetic storms appeared around solar maximum (Le & Liu 2020;Le et al. 2021b,c), indicating that solar sources for high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit are different from those for GLEs, strong SPEs and major geomagnetic storms.

Title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
Snippet: We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

Title: A Framework for Understanding and Quantifying the Loss and Acceleration of Relativistic Electrons in the Outer Radiation Belt During Geomagnetic Storms
Snippet: In this study we use previously identified storms compiled from Denton and Borovsky (2006), Kataoka and Miyoshi et al., (2006) and Hutchinson et al. (2011) to study dynamics of the outer radiation belt as characterized by the RBC index during CME and CIR driven storms. The Denton and Borovsky (2006) database contains 124 CIR driven storms between 1993-2005 that are selected based on prevailing solar wind conditions. Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006)identified isolated storms by a decrease in Dst below -100 nT and further characterized the predominant solar wind driver as either a CME or CIR related. This list comprises 55 storms, 49 CME driven storms and 6 CIRs. The Hutchinson et al. (2011)] storm list contains 143 storms, 104 CME driven storms and 39 CIR driven storms. Hutchinson et al. (2011) used the characteristic response of Sym-H to characterize geomagnetic storms; events were selected if they exhibited an initial phase (or sudden commencement), main phase and recovery phase. The prevailing solar wind conditions were then used to further subdivide these events into CME and CIR driven storms. 

In each of these three storm lists, no geomagnetic storm is identified based on the dynamics of the outer radiation belt and thus there is no assumed a priori response of the outer radiation belt. 

In our study we consider only storms where SAMPEX, OMNI, and ground-based magnetometer data are all available. Both OMNI and ground-based magnetometer data are used to analyse changes in RBC and thus are required for subsequent analysis. We also remove duplicate and overlapping storms, as defined by the storm start and end times (below). This leaves a total of 64 storms, 29 CME driven storms and 35 CIR driven storms. 

For each of the 64 storms we identify two distinct times; the start of the storm and the end of the storm determined by enhanced solar wind driving and storm-time Dst in a similar manner to Murphy et al. (2018).

(2017) also compared and contrasted 28 CME-driven versus 31 CIR-driven storms using Van Allen Probes data at three L-shell ranges in the outer belt; they found notable differences, including that CMEs drive enhancements of electrons that are most intense at lower L-shells compared to enhancements in CIR storms.

documents.snippet: It has found that most of major geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −100 nT) were CME-driven storms, while storms with Dst > −100 nT can be both CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms (Gosling et al. 1991;Richardson et al. 2002). Differences between CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms have been studied by Borovsky & Denton (2006). Some CME-driven storms were accompanied with solar proton events (SPEs). For example, about 80% of the great geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −200 nT) during solar cycles 23 were accompanied with SPEs (Le et al. 2016). In this context, CME-driven storms pose more threaten to the instruments on spaceships, astronauts in space stations, and Earth-based power grid systems. Many articles were devoted to the study of the relationship between CIR-driven storms and the environment of electrons of radiation belt (e.g., Borovsky & Denton 2006;Shen et al. 2017;Pandya et al. 2019, and reference therein). CIR-driven storms are more effect for the accelation of electrons in the region with L > 3.5 than CME-driven storms (Miyoshi & Kataoka 2005). The longer duration of CIR-driven storms, would accelerate electrons to higher energies, cause stronger spacecraft charging, and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons in the outer radiation belt (Borovsky & Denton 2006). The events of high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit did not appear around solar maximum (Le et al. 2021a). However, most of GLEs, strong SPEs (peak flux ≥1000 pfu), and major geomagnetic storms appeared around solar maximum (Le & Liu 2020;Le et al. 2021b,c), indicating that solar sources for high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit are different from those for GLEs, strong SPEs and major geomagnetic storms.

documents.title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
documents.snippet:
We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

documents.title: A Framework for Understanding and Quantifying the Loss and Acceleration of Relativistic Electrons in the Outer Radiation Belt During Geomagnetic Storms
documents.snippet:
In this study we use previously identified storms compiled from Denton and Borovsky (2006), Kataoka and Miyoshi et al., (2006) and Hutchinson et al. (2011) to study dynamics of the outer radiation belt as characterized by the RBC index during CME and CIR driven storms. The Denton and Borovsky (2006) database contains 124 CIR driven storms between 1993-2005 that are selected based on prevailing solar wind conditions. Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006)identified isolated storms by a decrease in Dst below -100 nT and further characterized the predominant solar wind driver as either a CME or CIR related. This list comprises 55 storms, 49 CME driven storms and 6 CIRs. The Hutchinson et al. (2011)] storm list contains 143 storms, 104 CME driven storms and 39 CIR driven storms. Hutchinson et al. (2011) used the characteristic response of Sym-H to characterize geomagnetic storms; events were selected if they exhibited an initial phase (or sudden commencement), main phase and recovery phase. The prevailing solar wind conditions were then used to further subdivide these events into CME and CIR driven storms. 

In each of these three storm lists, no geomagnetic storm is identified based on the dynamics of the outer radiation belt and thus there is no assumed a priori response of the outer radiation belt. 

In our study we consider only storms where SAMPEX, OMNI, and ground-based magnetometer data are all available. Both OMNI and ground-based magnetometer data are used to analyse changes in RBC and thus are required for subsequent analysis. We also remove duplicate and overlapping storms, as defined by the storm start and end times (below). This leaves a total of 64 storms, 29 CME driven storms and 35 CIR driven storms. 

For each of the 64 storms we identify two distinct times; the start of the storm and the end of the storm determined by enhanced solar wind driving and storm-time Dst in a similar manner to Murphy et al. (2018).

( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms.
