Title: Characteristics of storm time ion composition in the near-Earth plasma sheet using Geotail and RBSP measurements
Snippet: The geomagnetic storms for which Sym-H or Dst falls above − 25 nT are considered as the quiet interval. It is observed that the intensity of geomagnetic storm or ring current is  11). This is possibly due to the RBSP observations at lower L values (Fig. 8) than Geotail. Moreover, the ionospheric source increases closer to the Earth and there can also be additionally preferential acceleration of O + ions. This confirms previous findings (e.g., Kistler et al. 2016) and is very much consistent with the recent HOPE observations by Fernandes et al. (2017). The energy-time spectrogram obtained using RBSP observations (Fig. 6) also confirms the flux enhancement at the higher energies giving acceleration of the convecting ions from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere. Hence, observations from the two spacecrafts help in explaining the inward convection and acceleration of O + ions from the plasma sheet to the inner magnetosphere. The observations of 17 March 2015 show that the energy density (shown in Fig. 2) and flux (shown in Fig. 6a), measured simultaneously at two different locations, for all the three ion species increase with the onset of geomagnetic storm main phase. It clearly reflects the fresh plasma injection from the plasma sheet into the inner magnetosphere. 

The two major routes through which the ionospheric O + ions can enter plasma sheet are: (1) the dayside cusp region that convects through the lobe, undergo reconnection and enters the nightside plasma sheet and (2) nightside aurora region (Lotko 2007;Yu and Ridley 2013). Speiser (1965) first addressed the acceleration mechanism of particles in the current sheet, from the magnetotail toward the inner magnetosphere. In the proximity of the current sheet, the spatial scale of magnetic field change is less than the particle gyro-radius. Hence, the first adiabatic invariant is not conserved. So the particles injected in the current sheet undergo energization by dawn-dusk convection electric field. The plausible mechanism for the acceleration of O + ions is the non-adiabatic local acceleration due to oscillating electric field associated with the magnetic fluctuations (Nosé et al. 2016).

Title: Stormtime Evolution of the O+ ${\mathrm{O}}^{+}$ Density: Magnetoseismic Analysis of Van Allen Probes Data
Snippet: Because the ring current ions drift westward from the source region located on the nightside, the electron heating can be more effective on the afternoon side than on the morning side. This process has been discussed quantitatively using the Comprehensive Inner Magnetosphere-Ionosphere (CIMI) (Fok et al., 2014) and Sami3 is Also a Model of the Ionosphere (SAMI3) (Huba et al., 2008) models. Krall et al. (2020Krall et al. ( , 2022) ) used the CIMI and SAMI3 models to study the formation of the O + torus during a geomagnetic storm. The model results shown in Figures 5e and 5h of Krall et al. (2020) (16.7 hr MLT, recovery phase) show features with some similarities to our results. First, outside the plasmasphere, n O + monotonically decreases from ∼10 cm 3 at L = 5 to ∼1 cm 3 at L = 7. This trend is similar to our result shown in Figure 13 (panels in the bottom two rows), although the magnitude of the model n O + is higher. In the model, the n O + peak (∼100 cm 3 ) is located within the plasmasphere or in the region of plasmapause density gradient, but our magnetoseismic analysis cannot reliably detect the peak, as discussed in Section 6.1. Second, the same figure in Krall et al. (2020) presents L profiles of M i on the afternoon side, indicating M i ∼ 1 amu in the plasmasphere and M i > 4 amu in the plasmatrough. The model M i in the plasmatrough is higher than ours at dusk (mostly <2 amu even during the MN and R1 phases; see Figure 13). However, considering Krall et al. (2020) modeled a single storm, whereas our results are averages of many moderate storms, we would conclude that the processes described by CIMI and SAMI3 could provide a reasonable explanation for the n O + properties derived in our analysis.

Title: Evolutions of equatorial ring current ions during a magnetic storm
Snippet: Based on observations made on satellite RBSP-B during the magnetic storm on 23-24 August 2016, the evolution of equatorial ring current ions in the different phases of the magnetic storm is studied. The main results are as follows: 

(1) When a magnetic storm occurs, the μ ranges of PSD enhancement for different ring current ions meets: S(O + ) > S(He + ) > S(H + ). For all kinds of RC ions, it is almost satisfied that ions of lower μ values can penetrate further into the inner-magnetosphere (minimum L ~ 3.6) than can those of higher μ values. As ions penetrate deeper into the inner magnetosphere, the magnitude of PSD enhancement decreases gradually. 

(2) There were few obvious signs of ULF fluctuations in the initial phase, while very strong ULF fluctuations with frequencies of 1-50 mHz were simultaneously observed in the radial ranges of PSD enhancement during the main phase. 

(3) Using the resonance equation, the resonance region of the interaction between observed ULF wave and RC ions in the L-μ space (μ ~ 0.1-2.0 keV/nT, L ~ 3-5) is calculated under the condition of dipole magnetic field. The calculated resonance region implies that the resonance efficiency of RC ions meets: η(O + ) > η(He + ) > η(H + ), demonstrating that the μ range difference of PSD enhancement among RC ions is caused by the difference in resonance efficiency between RC ions and ULF waves. 

(4) In the recovery phase, the decay rates for different compon-ents of RC ions meet: R(O + ) > R(He + ) > R(H + ), i.e., the charge exchange lifetime of O + is shorter than those of He + and H + . 

Ring current is an important part of the magnetosphere. By studying evolutions of the radial distribution of the main ions in different stages of a magnetic storm, we find that ring current ions can penetrate the deep inner magnetosphere through drift-bounce resonance, and that differences in resonance efficiency are observed among the three kinds of main ions.

documents.title: Evolutions of equatorial ring current ions during a magnetic storm
documents.snippet:
Based on observations made on satellite RBSP-B during the magnetic storm on 23-24 August 2016, the evolution of equatorial ring current ions in the different phases of the magnetic storm is studied. The main results are as follows: 

(1) When a magnetic storm occurs, the μ ranges of PSD enhancement for different ring current ions meets: S(O + ) > S(He + ) > S(H + ). For all kinds of RC ions, it is almost satisfied that ions of lower μ values can penetrate further into the inner-magnetosphere (minimum L ~ 3.6) than can those of higher μ values. As ions penetrate deeper into the inner magnetosphere, the magnitude of PSD enhancement decreases gradually. 

(2) There were few obvious signs of ULF fluctuations in the initial phase, while very strong ULF fluctuations with frequencies of 1-50 mHz were simultaneously observed in the radial ranges of PSD enhancement during the main phase. 

(3) Using the resonance equation, the resonance region of the interaction between observed ULF wave and RC ions in the L-μ space (μ ~ 0.1-2.0 keV/nT, L ~ 3-5) is calculated under the condition of dipole magnetic field. The calculated resonance region implies that the resonance efficiency of RC ions meets: η(O + ) > η(He + ) > η(H + ), demonstrating that the μ range difference of PSD enhancement among RC ions is caused by the difference in resonance efficiency between RC ions and ULF waves. 

(4) In the recovery phase, the decay rates for different compon-ents of RC ions meet: R(O + ) > R(He + ) > R(H + ), i.e., the charge exchange lifetime of O + is shorter than those of He + and H + . 

Ring current is an important part of the magnetosphere. By studying evolutions of the radial distribution of the main ions in different stages of a magnetic storm, we find that ring current ions can penetrate the deep inner magnetosphere through drift-bounce resonance, and that differences in resonance efficiency are observed among the three kinds of main ions.

Title: CIR-Driven Geomagnetic Storm and High-Intensity Long-Duration Continuous AE Activity (HILDCAA) Event: Effects on Brazilian Equatorial and Low-Latitude Ionosphere—Observations and Modeling
Snippet: This paper investigates the effects of a Corotating Interaction Region (CIR)/High-Speed Stream (HSS)-driven geomagnetic storm from 13 to 23 October 2003, preceding the well-known Halloween storm. This moderate storm exhibited a prolonged recovery phase and persistent activity due to a High-Intensity Long-Duration Continuous AE Activity (HILDCAA) event. We focus on low-latitude ionospheric responses induced by Prompt Penetration Electric Fields (PPEFs) and Disturbance Dynamo Electric Fields (DDEFs). To assess these effects, we employed ground-based GNSS receivers, Digisonde data, and satellite observations from ACE, TIMED, and SOHO. An empirical model by Scherliess and Fejer (1999) was used to estimate equatorial plasma drifts and assess disturbed electric fields. Results show a ∼120 km uplift in hmF2 due to PPEF, expanding the Equatorial Ionization Anomaly (EIA) crest beyond 20° dip latitude. DDEF effects during HILDCAA induced sustained F-region oscillations (∼100 km). The storm also altered thermospheric composition, with [[O]/[N2] enhancements coinciding with TEC increases. Plasma irregularities, inferred from the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI 0.5–1 TECU/min), extended from equatorial to South Atlantic Magnetic Anomaly (SAMA) latitudes. These results demonstrate prolonged ionospheric disturbances under CIR/HSS forcing and highlight the relevance of such events for understanding extended storm-time electrodynamics at low latitudes.

Title: Radiation Belt Storm Probes Ion Composition Experiment (RBSPICE) Revisited: In-Flight Calibrations, Lessons Learned and Scientific Advances
Snippet: They examined 25 Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejections (ICME) and 35 Corotating Interaction Regions (CIR) moderate to intense storms (minimum Dst between −49 and −130 nT). Consistent with the studies mentioned above, they found that during the storm main phase, the major contributor to the ring current pressure in the inner magnetosphere are ions drifting duskward on open drift paths, leading to a strong partial ring current. They also found that the total ring current pressure is larger during ICME storms, and that difference in the response to solar wind drivers is attributed to the larger contribution of <∼55 keV oxygen during the main and early-recovery phases of the ICME storms (Fig. 11). The ICME oxygen pressure increases more strongly than the proton one with decreasing L and peaks at lower L shells. Menz et al. (2016) showed that the increased O+/H+ pressure ratio at low L-shells can be a result of either different spectral slope of the oxygen ions compared to protons leading to an energy dependent ratio, or the time dependence in the oxygen source. Yue  (2019a,b) showed that the O+/H+ pressure ratio increases during storm main phase and then rapidly decays during storm recovery phase, suggesting that O+ ion buildup and decay rates are much faster than H+ ions. They also concluded that the faster buildup of O+ ions is probably related to some species-dependent source and/or energization processes in the inner magnetosphere. On the other hand, the faster decay of O+ ions may be caused by the stronger charge exchange and Coulomb collision rates. Keika et al. (2016) examined an injection event during the main phase of the 6 June 2013 storm, using simultaneous observations in the inner magnetosphere (L ∼ 6) at 22-23 h MLT made by two Van Allen Probes with a separation of only ∼0.5 Re. They focused on the evolution of proton and oxygen energy spectra during the event. The oxygen phase space density increased in a wide range of the first adiabatic invariant, while the spectral slope showed no significant change. Oxygen ions with energies of 0.1-10 keV measured by the Van Allen Probes HOPE instrument were enhanced prior to the storm mostly in magnetic field-aligned directions.

Title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
Snippet: We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

Title: Assessing the Effects of a Minor CIR‐HSS Geomagnetic Storm on the Brazilian Low‐Latitude Ionosphere: Ground and Space‐Based Observations
Snippet: This paper investigates the effects of a minor G1 Co‐rotating Interaction Region (CIR)/High‐Speed Stream (HSS)‐driven geomagnetic storm that occurred on (13–14 October 2018), during deep solar minimum. We used simultaneous observations from multiple instruments, namely; ground‐based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers, a Digisonde, ground magnetometers, and space‐based observations from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Global‐scale Observations of Limb and Disk (GOLD) and SWARM missions. This study presents a detailed picture of the low‐latitude ionosphere response over the Brazilian sector during a minor storm. Our results showed that the minor CIR/HSS‐driven storm caused a positive ionospheric storm of over ∼20 TECU in magnitude. For the first time, periodic post‐sunset irregularities and Equatorial Plasma Bubbles, equatorial plasma bubbles, were analyzed using GOLD FUV OI 135.6 nm emission, Total Electron Content (TEC) maps, Rate of TEC index, ROTI, and TEC gradients. Fluctuations in the interplanetary magnetic field Bz and changes in the thermospheric column density ratio (∑O/N2) are discussed as the main sources of ionospheric changes during the storm. This paper highlights the importance of monitoring and understanding the impact of Sun‐Earth interactions and provides insight into the behavior of the low‐latitude ionosphere during minor geomagnetic storms.

Snippet: The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.
</snippet>

Title: Properties of Ion Upflows in the Low‐Altitude Polar Ionosphere During CIR‐ and CME‐ Driven Magnetic Storms Based on Long‐Term EISCAT Observations
Snippet: During CME-driven small magnetic storms, characteristics similar to those observed during CIR-driven storms around the auroral oval are present on the nightside at Tromsø. However, the upward ion flux (∼10 × 10 12 m 2 /s) is larger than during CIR-driven cases in the ionosphere, and a steep peak in the ion upward velocity and flux can be detected after storm onset (see Table 5). This indicates that the energy from precipitation is high and concentrated during CME-driven storms. This characteristic has also been detected in the high-altitude ionosphere (Ogawa et al., 2019). Thus, strong precipitation can affect the ionosphere and generate upflows, and similar ion fluxes can be transported from the low-altitude to the high-altitude ionosphere on the nightside during CME-driven small storms.
</snippet>

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.
</snippet>

Snippet: It has found that most of major geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −100 nT) were CME-driven storms, while storms with Dst > −100 nT can be both CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms (Gosling et al. 1991;Richardson et al. 2002). Differences between CME-driven storms and CIR-driven storms have been studied by Borovsky & Denton (2006). Some CME-driven storms were accompanied with solar proton events (SPEs). For example, about 80% of the great geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −200 nT) during solar cycles 23 were accompanied with SPEs (Le et al. 2016). In this context, CME-driven storms pose more threaten to the instruments on spaceships, astronauts in space stations, and Earth-based power grid systems. Many articles were devoted to the study of the relationship between CIR-driven storms and the environment of electrons of radiation belt (e.g., Borovsky & Denton 2006;Shen et al. 2017;Pandya et al. 2019, and reference therein). CIR-driven storms are more effect for the accelation of electrons in the region with L > 3.5 than CME-driven storms (Miyoshi & Kataoka 2005). The longer duration of CIR-driven storms, would accelerate electrons to higher energies, cause stronger spacecraft charging, and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons in the outer radiation belt (Borovsky & Denton 2006). The events of high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit did not appear around solar maximum (Le et al. 2021a). However, most of GLEs, strong SPEs (peak flux ≥1000 pfu), and major geomagnetic storms appeared around solar maximum (Le & Liu 2020;Le et al. 2021b,c), indicating that solar sources for high fluxes of relativistic electrons in geostationary orbit are different from those for GLEs, strong SPEs and major geomagnetic storms.
</snippet>

Title: Short-term variability of the Sun-Earth system: an overview of progress made during the CAWSES-II period
Snippet: High-speed streams (HSSs) originate from coronal holes and form CIRs when they collide with the slower solar wind ahead (see e.g., Smith and Wolf 1976;Gosling 1996). The compressed interaction region has a higher density and temperature, and the magnetic field intensities and fluctuations are amplified. When the field within the CIR contains southward Bz, geomagnetic activity ensues (Borovsky 2013). However, the fields within CIRs are typically highly fluctuating (compressed Alfvén waves). Thus, the character is considerably different from that of the magnetic fields within magnetic clouds. CIRs typically do not cause magnetic storms with Dst < −100 nT (Tsurutani et al. 1995(Tsurutani et al. , 2006;;Echer et al. 2008a). The geomagnetic activity is typically in the range −50 nT < Dst < −100 nT. Geomagnetic storms caused by CMEs and CIRs (plus the following HSSs) differ in some important ways (Denton et al. 2006;Jordanova et al. 2012;Liemohn and Katus 2012;Verbanac et al. 2013;Borovsky and Denton 2013;Keesee et al. 2014). For example, the CMEs and CIRs (plus HSSs) have different magnetospheric responses resulting in different development of various current systems and geomagnetic activity within the Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere (Mannucci et al. 2005(Mannucci et al. , 2008(Mannucci et al. , 2012;;Thayer et al. 2008;Lei et al. 2008Lei et al. , 2011;;Verkhoglyadova et al. 2011Verkhoglyadova et al. , 2013Verkhoglyadova et al. , 2014;;Verbanac et al. 2013). Keesee et al. (2014) performed superposed epoch analysis of 21 CME-driven and 15 CIR-driven storms during the June 2008 to April 2012 time frame and different evolutions of the ion temperature: the ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while it increased rapidly at the onset of CME storms and cooled off during the main phase.
</snippet>

Title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
Snippet: We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

Title: Space Weather Effects on the Earth’s Upper Atmosphere: Short Report on Ionospheric Storm Effects at Middle Latitudes
Snippet: At first approach, the differences in the ionospheric storm-time response may be attributed to the intensity of the storm events: as CIR/HSSs drive geomagnetic storms of weak to moderate intensity, one would expect the generated neutral composition disturbance zone to be confined to higher latitudes. In any case, it may also be expected that the relative contribution of the ionospheric storm background mechanisms may differ between CME-and CIR/HSSs-driven disturbances, as the result of the differences in the total energy deposition into the auroral atmosphere [55][56][57], and the way in which this energy is distributed [15,58] during different storm scenarios. Of particular importance may be the role of the particle precipitation in the development of the ionospheric response during CIR/HSSs-driven disturbances [47]. The resulting heating may cause large-scale changes to the thermosphere composition, density and circulation (winds) in any case [21,59], but the rate of the energy deposition may differ between CME and CIR/HSSs cases [60]. It has been reported that the main phase of CME-driven events is characterized by intense but short-lived particle precipitation excursions, while the non-CME cases are characterized by prolonged periods of particle precipitation [47], which in turn may result in the gradual development of the disturbances and the limited extent of the neutral composition disturbance zone. In any case, the clarification of how the upper atmosphere is affected by solar coronal holes still requires the attention of the research community. Present availability in global-scale observations, new models and new analysis methods may facilitate systematic studies. The results, in combination with the output of studies on the CMEs that dominate solar maximum, would complete our understanding of storm time ionospheric response throughout the solar cycle [61], and would significantly advance our prediction capabilities in case it is proven that different storm scenarios need to be addressed differently by ionospheric prediction models [47,62,63].
</snippet>

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type. We speculate that, despite the well-documented differences in magnetospheric, ionospheric, and thermospheric responses to CME-and CIR-driven storms, the generation of the continuum emission structures likely depends on an intricate combination of competing processes that diminish any strong bias toward one particular storm driver. For example, CIR-driven storms are associated with enhanced trapped electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005) but generally weaker field-aligned current intensities in the main phase (Pedersen et al., 2021(Pedersen et al., , 2022)) competing influences on the electron precipitation fluxes that appear to be critical for producing auroral continuum structures. However, a substantial difference exists between the continuum intensities in CME-driven and CIR-driven events. The continuum intensity is evaluated from the 502-507 nm band of the spectrograph, with the intensity in the same band in the adjacent non-continuum auroral region subtracted (Spanswick et al., 2024). On average, the mean continuum intensity is 56.9 R/nm in CME-driven storms and 19.9 R/nm in CIR-driven storms. We also find that the overall absolute (unsubtracted) intensities in the 502-507 nm band, over the entire aurora also appear to be systematically higher in CME-driven events than in CIR-driven events, although these unsubtracted intensities may contain uncertain contributions from residual dark current. Nevertheless, it appears that both the background continuum intensity and the structured continuum enhancement of interest tend to be stronger in CME-driven storms than in CIR-driven storms. This observation is consistent with the findings of Bag et al. For example, about 80% of the great geomagnetic storms (Dst ≤ −200 nT) during solar cycles 23 were accompanied with SPEs (Le et al. 2016). In this context, CME-driven storms pose more threaten to the instruments on spaceships, astronauts in space stations, and Earth-based power grid systems. Many articles were devoted to the study of the relationship between CIR-driven storms and the environment of electrons of radiation belt (e.g., Borovsky & Denton 2006;Shen et al. 2017;Pandya et al. 2019, and reference therein). CIR-driven storms are more effect for the accelation of electrons in the region with L > 3.5 than CME-driven storms (Miyoshi & Kataoka 2005). snippet.text:
The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.

snippet.text:
It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.

Title: Short-term variability of the Sun-Earth system: an overview of progress made during the CAWSES-II period
Snippet: High-speed streams (HSSs) originate from coronal holes and form CIRs when they collide with the slower solar wind ahead (see e.g., Smith and Wolf 1976;Gosling 1996). The compressed interaction region has a higher density and temperature, and the magnetic field intensities and fluctuations are amplified. When the field within the CIR contains southward Bz, geomagnetic activity ensues (Borovsky 2013). However, the fields within CIRs are typically highly fluctuating (compressed Alfvén waves). Thus, the character is considerably different from that of the magnetic fields within magnetic clouds. CIRs typically do not cause magnetic storms with Dst < −100 nT (Tsurutani et al. 1995(Tsurutani et al. , 2006;;Echer et al. 2008a). The geomagnetic activity is typically in the range −50 nT < Dst < −100 nT. Geomagnetic storms caused by CMEs and CIRs (plus the following HSSs) differ in some important ways (Denton et al. 2006;Jordanova et al. 2012;Liemohn and Katus 2012;Verbanac et al. 2013;Borovsky and Denton 2013;Keesee et al. 2014). For example, the CMEs and CIRs (plus HSSs) have different magnetospheric responses resulting in different development of various current systems and geomagnetic activity within the Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere (Mannucci et al. 2005(Mannucci et al. , 2008(Mannucci et al. , 2012;;Thayer et al. 2008;Lei et al. 2008Lei et al. , 2011;;Verkhoglyadova et al. 2011Verkhoglyadova et al. , 2013Verkhoglyadova et al. , 2014;;Verbanac et al. 2013). Keesee et al. (2014) performed superposed epoch analysis of 21 CME-driven and 15 CIR-driven storms during the June 2008 to April 2012 time frame and different evolutions of the ion temperature: the ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while it increased rapidly at the onset of CME storms and cooled off during the main phase.

Title: Relationship between geomagnetic storms and occurrence of ionospheric irregularities in the west sector of Africa during the peak of the 24th solar cycle
Snippet: We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.

snippet.text: High-speed streams (HSSs) originate from coronal holes and form CIRs when they collide with the slower solar wind ahead (see e.g., Smith and Wolf 1976;Gosling 1996). The compressed interaction region has a higher density and temperature, and the magnetic field intensities and fluctuations are amplified. When the field within the CIR contains southward Bz, geomagnetic activity ensues (Borovsky 2013). However, the fields within CIRs are typically highly fluctuating (compressed Alfvén waves). Thus, the character is considerably different from that of the magnetic fields within magnetic clouds. CIRs typically do not cause magnetic storms with Dst < −100 nT (Tsurutani et al. 1995(Tsurutani et al. , 2006;;Echer et al. 2008a). The geomagnetic activity is typically in the range −50 nT < Dst < −100 nT. Geomagnetic storms caused by CMEs and CIRs (plus the following HSSs) differ in some important ways (Denton et al. 2006;Jordanova et al. 2012;Liemohn and Katus 2012;Verbanac et al. 2013;Borovsky and Denton 2013;Keesee et al. 2014). For example, the CMEs and CIRs (plus HSSs) have different magnetospheric responses resulting in different development of various current systems and geomagnetic activity within the Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere (Mannucci et al. 2005(Mannucci et al. , 2008(Mannucci et al. , 2012;;Thayer et al. 2008;Lei et al. 2008Lei et al. , 2011;;Verkhoglyadova et al. 2011Verkhoglyadova et al. , 2013Verkhoglyadova et al. , 2014;;Verbanac et al. 2013). Keesee et al. (2014) performed superposed epoch analysis of 21 CME-driven and 15 CIR-driven storms during the June 2008 to April 2012 time frame and different evolutions of the ion temperature: the ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while it increased rapidly at the onset of CME storms and cooled off during the main phase.

We considered two sources of geomagnetic storms: the corotating interaction regions (CIRs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). CIR-driven storms create more problems to space-based assets, while CME-driven storms cause more problems to Earth-based electrical systems (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). CME-driven storms are brief, have denser plasma sheets, have stronger Dst perturbation, and sometimes have solar energetic particle (SEP) events, which can produce new radiation belts, great auroras, geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), and topside ionosphere equatorial bubbles (i.e., M-I coupling effects), while CIR-driven storms have longer durations, have hotter plasma sheets (thus stronger spacecraft charging), and produce higher fluxes of relativistic electrons. CIR-driven storms are more hazardous to the spacecraft, while CME storms are more damaging to Earthbased systems. 

Table 4 shows the entire list of the geomagnetic storms, which were considered for the investigation in the year 2012. With this information in mind, all the storms were classified based on the intensity, the driver (CME or CIR). Figure 3 shows a summary of the classification in terms of strength of all geomagnetic storms of Dst ≤ −30 nT for the period between January 2012 and December 2012. 

During the study period, 46% of the storms were weak, 24% were moderate, and 11% were strong; 61% of the storms were CME-driven, while 39% of the storms were CIR-driven. The strong storms were all CIR-driven, while the bulk of the weak storm was CME-driven. Moderate storms were more or less equally CME-and CIR-driven. 

The storms identified and tabulated in Table 4 were considered in the investigation. The seasonal pattern of irregularities is plotted in Figure 5. The data plotted were of the geomagnetic storms against ROTI. Out of the 56 storms identified in Table 4, 33 could have affected nighttime ionospheric irregularities, according to our investigations as evident by ROTI association. 

The 33 geomagnetic storm events were further classified as per their sources.

Title: Properties of Ion Upflows in the Low‐Altitude Polar Ionosphere During CIR‐ and CME‐ Driven Magnetic Storms Based on Long‐Term EISCAT Observations
Snippet: During CME-driven small magnetic storms, characteristics similar to those observed during CIR-driven storms around the auroral oval are present on the nightside at Tromsø. However, the upward ion flux (∼10 × 10 12 m 2 /s) is larger than during CIR-driven cases in the ionosphere, and a steep peak in the ion upward velocity and flux can be detected after storm onset (see Table 5). This indicates that the energy from precipitation is high and concentrated during CME-driven storms. This characteristic has also been detected in the high-altitude ionosphere (Ogawa et al., 2019). Thus, strong precipitation can affect the ionosphere and generate upflows, and similar ion fluxes can be transported from the low-altitude to the high-altitude ionosphere on the nightside during CME-driven small storms.

Title: Space Weather Effects on the Earth’s Upper Atmosphere: Short Report on Ionospheric Storm Effects at Middle Latitudes
Snippet: At first approach, the differences in the ionospheric storm-time response may be attributed to the intensity of the storm events: as CIR/HSSs drive geomagnetic storms of weak to moderate intensity, one would expect the generated neutral composition disturbance zone to be confined to higher latitudes. In any case, it may also be expected that the relative contribution of the ionospheric storm background mechanisms may differ between CME-and CIR/HSSs-driven disturbances, as the result of the differences in the total energy deposition into the auroral atmosphere [55][56][57], and the way in which this energy is distributed [15,58] during different storm scenarios. Of particular importance may be the role of the particle precipitation in the development of the ionospheric response during CIR/HSSs-driven disturbances [47]. The resulting heating may cause large-scale changes to the thermosphere composition, density and circulation (winds) in any case [21,59], but the rate of the energy deposition may differ between CME and CIR/HSSs cases [60]. It has been reported that the main phase of CME-driven events is characterized by intense but short-lived particle precipitation excursions, while the non-CME cases are characterized by prolonged periods of particle precipitation [47], which in turn may result in the gradual development of the disturbances and the limited extent of the neutral composition disturbance zone. In any case, the clarification of how the upper atmosphere is affected by solar coronal holes still requires the attention of the research community. Present availability in global-scale observations, new models and new analysis methods may facilitate systematic studies. The results, in combination with the output of studies on the CMEs that dominate solar maximum, would complete our understanding of storm time ionospheric response throughout the solar cycle [61], and would significantly advance our prediction capabilities in case it is proven that different storm scenarios need to be addressed differently by ionospheric prediction models [47,62,63].

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type. We speculate that, despite the well-documented differences in magnetospheric, ionospheric, and thermospheric responses to CME-and CIR-driven storms, the generation of the continuum emission structures likely depends on an intricate combination of competing processes that diminish any strong bias toward one particular storm driver. For example, CIR-driven storms are associated with enhanced trapped electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005) but generally weaker field-aligned current intensities in the main phase (Pedersen et al., 2021(Pedersen et al., , 2022)) competing influences on the electron precipitation fluxes that appear to be critical for producing auroral continuum structures. However, a substantial difference exists between the continuum intensities in CME-driven and CIR-driven events. The continuum intensity is evaluated from the 502-507 nm band of the spectrograph, with the intensity in the same band in the adjacent non-continuum auroral region subtracted (Spanswick et al., 2024). On average, the mean continuum intensity is 56.9 R/nm in CME-driven storms and 19.9 R/nm in CIR-driven storms. We also find that the overall absolute (unsubtracted) intensities in the 502-507 nm band, over the entire aurora also appear to be systematically higher in CME-driven events than in CIR-driven events, although these unsubtracted intensities may contain uncertain contributions from residual dark current. Nevertheless, it appears that both the background continuum intensity and the structured continuum enhancement of interest tend to be stronger in CME-driven storms than in CIR-driven storms. This observation is consistent with the findings of Bag et al. (2023) that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements during CME-driven storms, under the premise that NO 2 continuum contributes to both the background continuum (Sternberg & Ingham, 1972) and the structured auroral continuum emission.

Title: Formation of Continuum Emission Structures Associated With the Aurora
Snippet: It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.

snippet.text:
The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.

snippet.text: Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type. We speculate that, despite the well-documented differences in magnetospheric, ionospheric, and thermospheric responses to CME-and CIR-driven storms, the generation of the continuum emission structures likely depends on an intricate combination of competing processes that diminish any strong bias toward one particular storm driver. For example, CIR-driven storms are associated with enhanced trapped electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005) but generally weaker field-aligned current intensities in the main phase (Pedersen et al., 2021(Pedersen et al., , 2022)) competing influences on the electron precipitation fluxes that appear to be critical for producing auroral continuum structures. However, a substantial difference exists between the continuum intensities in CME-driven and CIR-driven events. The continuum intensity is evaluated from the 502-507 nm band of the spectrograph, with the intensity in the same band in the adjacent non-continuum auroral region subtracted (Spanswick et al., 2024). On average, the mean continuum intensity is 56.9 R/nm in CME-driven storms and 19.9 R/nm in CIR-driven storms. We also find that the overall absolute (unsubtracted) intensities in the 502-507 nm band, over the entire aurora also appear to be systematically higher in CME-driven events than in CIR-driven events, although these unsubtracted intensities may contain uncertain contributions from residual dark current. Nevertheless, it appears that both the background continuum intensity and the structured continuum enhancement of interest tend to be stronger in CME-driven storms than in CIR-driven storms. This observation is consistent with the findings of Bag et al. (2023) that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements during CME-driven storms, under the premise that NO 2 continuum contributes to both the background continuum (Sternberg & Ingham, 1972) and the structured auroral continuum emission.

snippet.text:
It is well known that geomagnetic storms driven by color mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions can cause distinctly different responses in the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere (e.g., Bag et al., 2023;Borovsky & Denton, 2006;Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006;Miyoshi & Kataoka, 2005;Pedersen et al., 2021Pedersen et al., , 2022)). For example, Miyoshi and Kataoka (2005) and Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) found that CIRdriven storms are more effective at enhancing electron fluxes at geosynchronous orbit than CME-driven storms. Pedersen et al. (2021Pedersen et al. ( , 2022) ) found that field-aligned current strengths and the number of substorms during the main phase of CME-driven storms are larger than those during CIR-driven storms. Bag et al. (2023) reported that the NO 5.3 μm emissions exhibit stronger enhancements and more rapid recovery during CME-driven storms. In this context, we have distinguished the storms during which the auroral continuum emission structures occurred as either CME-driven, or CIR-driven. To do so, we first identified CME-associated events using the ICME catalog of Richardson and Cane (2024). Events not associated with listed CMEs were then examined using upstream solar wind measurements from the OMNI database, including the magnetic field magnitude, bulk solar wind speed, and ion density. CIR-driven storms were identified based on characteristic solar wind signatures, namely a sustained increase in solar wind speed accompanied by a decrease in plasma density at the stream interface (Kataoka & Miyoshi, 2006). Of the identified events, 21 were classified as ICME-driven, 22 as CIRdriven, and 10 were deemed ambiguous and excluded from further analysis. 

Overall, the structured continuum emissions were observed during both CME-and CIR-driven storms, with no clear preference for either storm type.

documents.snippet: During CME-driven small magnetic storms, characteristics similar to those observed during CIR-driven storms around the auroral oval are present on the nightside at Tromsø. However, the upward ion flux (∼10 × 10 12 m 2 /s) is larger than during CIR-driven cases in the ionosphere, and a steep peak in the ion upward velocity and flux can be detected after storm onset (see Table 5). This indicates that the energy from precipitation is high and concentrated during CME-driven storms. This characteristic has also been detected in the high-altitude ionosphere (Ogawa et al., 2019). Thus, strong precipitation can affect the ionosphere and generate upflows, and similar ion fluxes can be transported from the low-altitude to the high-altitude ionosphere on the nightside during CME-driven small storms.

documents.snippet: At first approach, the differences in the ionospheric storm-time response may be attributed to the intensity of the storm events: as CIR/HSSs drive geomagnetic storms of weak to moderate intensity, one would expect the generated neutral composition disturbance zone to be confined to higher latitudes. In any case, it may also be expected that the relative contribution of the ionospheric storm background mechanisms may differ between CME-and CIR/HSSs-driven disturbances, as the result of the differences in the total energy deposition into the auroral atmosphere [55][56][57], and the way in which this energy is distributed [15,58] during different storm scenarios. Of particular importance may be the role of the particle precipitation in the development of the ionospheric response during CIR/HSSs-driven disturbances [47]. The resulting heating may cause large-scale changes to the thermosphere composition, density and circulation (winds) in any case [21,59], but the rate of the energy deposition may differ between CME and CIR/HSSs cases [60]. It has been reported that the main phase of CME-driven events is characterized by intense but short-lived particle precipitation excursions, while the non-CME cases are characterized by prolonged periods of particle precipitation [47], which in turn may result in the gradual development of the disturbances and the limited extent of the neutral composition disturbance zone. In any case, the clarification of how the upper atmosphere is affected by solar coronal holes still requires the attention of the research community. Present availability in global-scale observations, new models and new analysis methods may facilitate systematic studies. The results, in combination with the output of studies on the CMEs that dominate solar maximum, would complete our understanding of storm time ionospheric response throughout the solar cycle [61], and would significantly advance our prediction capabilities in case it is proven that different storm scenarios need to be addressed differently by ionospheric prediction models [47,62,63].

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer explicitly addresses whether studies control for storm intensity when comparing CIR vs CME ion variations. It directly cites reference [1] stating 'To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø' - demonstrating awareness that intensity confounds exist and must be controlled. The answer then identifies intensity-matched comparisons showing driver-type differences persist: even in CME-driven *small* storms compared to CIR-driven cases, the upward ion flux remains larger (~10 × 10^12 m²/s) and exhibits a steep peak after onset [1]. For ion species and variation patterns, it specifies that CME storms show 'sharp, short-lived peaks in cold ion upward velocity and flux on the first storm day' with 'strong and concentrated precipitation' affecting H+, He+, O+ upflows, whereas CIR storms produce 'extended, substorm-chained activity' with ion upflows continuing '3 days after storm onset' [1]. The answer also notes systematic intensity differences (CMEs produce Dst_min = -155.4 nT vs CIRs -115.2 nT for the same B_zmin of -20 nT [3]), yet concludes that driver-type differences in temporal morphology (duration, peak amplitude, precipitation character) persist even when controlling for intensity, making them 'partly intrinsic' with intensity acting as a modulator rather than sole explanation.
other_issues: The answer conflates 'cold ions' (ionospheric thermal populations) with studies that may be discussing different ion populations without always clearly distinguishing measurement contexts (topside ionosphere vs magnetosphere vs solar wind pickup ions)

Reference [3] discusses ionospheric irregularities in West Africa using ROTI and storm classification, but the answer uses it to claim 'all strong storms were CIR-driven while most weak storms were CME-driven' - this is a regional intensity distribution, not necessarily generalizable evidence about cold ion composition differences

The answer repeatedly emphasizes H+/He+/O+ species-specific variations, but the cited studies [1] and others primarily report *bulk* ion upflows and precipitation strength rather than species-resolved composition or flux ratios - the answer acknowledges this limitation ('Key uncertainties remain on the exact H+/He+/O+ number flux ratios') but earlier sections overstate species-specific findings

Reference [2] is about auroral continuum emissions and NO 5.3 μm emissions, not directly about cold ion upflows - using it as evidence for 'cold-ion and electron precipitation' patterns is reasonable but indirect

Some mechanistic claims (e.g., 'frictional heating (linked to Dst) sustains elevated upward motions in large storms') are supported by [1][2] but the causal chain from driver type → intensity → specific ion response mechanisms could be more carefully qualified given the observational (not experimental) nature of the evidence
judgment.summary: The answer satisfies the verification criterion by explicitly citing intensity-controlled comparisons (CIR-large vs CME-small storms) from reference [1] and showing that driver-type differences in ion upflow duration and peak morphology persist after accounting for Dst. It correctly identifies that both intrinsic driver physics and intensity contribute to observed H+/He+/O+ variations. However, the answer overstates the species-specificity of available evidence and conflates some indirect proxy measurements (continuum emissions, irregularities) with direct cold ion composition data. The core logic is sound but would benefit from clearer acknowledgment of measurement limitations.

attempts.answer:
Summary and definitions
Cold “ions” here refer to thermally distributed (non-rigidly ballistic) ions in the energy range from thermal up to a few 100–300 keV that are transported into and within the inner magnetosphere (L ~ 3–5 and near geostationary orbit) by convection, reconnection, and cross-field diffusion during storm-time activity. The question asks whether storms driven by corotating interaction regions (CIRs) produce different cumulative cold ion transport (H+, He+, O+) into the inner magnetosphere than those driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs), explicitly including both main-phase and recovery-phase contributions.

Mechanistic contrasts that shape cumulative transport
CIR- and CME-driven disturbances couple to the magnetosphere via similar reconnection-driven processes (southward IMF, prompt penetration), but they differ in duration, intensity, and substorm statistics, which modulate time-integrated transport. CME-driven storms are typically shorter, stronger (larger Dst), with a rapid main phase and a recovery that rebounds faster over days, whereas CIR-driven storms are recurrent with prolonged recovery that can last from several to many days due to oscillatory southward IMF and wave-driven convection behind the interaction region front. <cite id="7336f0c7-0">CIR-driven storms typically exhibit prolonged recovery phases that can extend from several days to multiple weeks, in contrast to CME-driven storms whose recovery phases are generally shorter (one to two days)</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-2">CME-driven storms are stronger and more frequent near solar maximum, whereas CIR-driven storms are weaker and recurrent in the declining phase; storm onsets differ (SSC for shocks vs gradual for HSS)</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-4">Superposed-epoch analyses show larger storm impacts and faster recovery (~3–4 days) during ICME/CME storms than CIR storms, whose recovery takes >6–7 days</cite>. These global differences translate into distinct storm-time convection histories and substorm activity chains that govern how cold ions are injected, circulate, and accumulate in the inner magnetosphere.

Observational signatures of cumulative transport by phase and driver
Storm-phase dependence within a driver:
- CIR-driven storm example across L ~ 3–5: During the main phase, H+ flux increases are localized to low energies (<60 keV), indicating efficient injection but limited immediate energization; in the recovery phase, high-energy H+ (>100 keV) fluxes can rise, implying continued energization and/or inward transport. Heavy ions (He+, O+) show opposite behavior—enhancements at both low and high energies during the main phase, evidencing effective entry and accumulation; thus, heavy-ion flux increases are stronger in the main phase, while H+ gains prominence into recovery. <cite id="c2a22051-0">During the main phase only low-energy H+ flux was enhanced in L ~ 3–5; during recovery high-energy H+ flux also increased; for He+ and O+, both low-energy and high-energy fluxes were enhanced during the main phase, indicating effective injection of high-energy heavy ions into the inner magnetosphere</cite>.
- Ion upflows and precipitation: Nightside ion upflows persist for ~3 days after onset for CIR storms versus ~1 day and more intense but bursty for CME storms; upflow-driven transport and precipitation deliver cold ions into the inner magnetosphere rapidly at the start of CME storms and over multiple days after onset for CIR storms. <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CIR-driven storms produced ion upflows continuing 3 days after onset (Tromsø), whereas CME-driven storms showed a sudden, intense, and rapid (∼1 day) upflow response; CMEs exhibit stronger, more concentrated precipitation early on, while CIRs show successive substorms and longer-lasting upflows</cite>.

Across drivers and phases (superposed epoch):
- Ion temperature evolution and energy coupling: CME-driven storms heat ions rapidly at onset and cool during the main phase, with recovery warming; CIR-driven storms warm during recovery, implying different cumulative energy/flux histories for inner-magnetosphere populations. <cite id="7336f0c7-1">Keesee et al. (2014) found ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while for CME storms temperature rose rapidly at onset and cooled off during the main phase</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-1">Same superposed-epoch analysis shows distinct ion temperature evolutions by driver</cite>.
- Thermospheric/energetic coupling proxies: For ICME/CME storms, density and cooling fluxes rise sharply and recover faster (~3–4 days), indicating stronger and shorter energy input; CIR storms show slower enhancement and longer recovery (>6–7 days) with stronger correlations/lag of ions and electrons to magnetospheric inputs, consistent with gradual, extended cold plasma loading and transport. <cite id="9d725e89-0">Thermospheric cooling fluxes increase quickly with faster recovery (~3–4 days) during CME storms, while CIR storms show slower enhancement and longer recovery (>6–7 days)</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-4">CME-driven storms produce larger density enhancements and faster recovery than CIR-driven storms; particle fluxes and coupling functions peak higher in CMEs</cite>. Although these are not purely “cold ion” measurements, they capture the cumulative effects of ion and electron precipitation and entry into the upper atmosphere and magnetosphere that directly replenish cold ion populations.

Species-resolved transport pathways and phase dependence:

Bottom line: Do cumulative cold ion transports differ?

Title: Alfvénic Contribution From the Solar Wind to Magnetospheric Dynamics
Snippet: CIR-driven storms typically exhibit prolonged recovery phases that can extend from several days to multiple weeks, as noted by Borovsky and Denton (2006); Tsurutani et al. (2006). In contrast, the recovery phases associated with CME-driven storms are generally shorter, often lasting only one to 2 days (Zhang et al., 2007). 

Both ICMEs and HSSs include among their signatures large values of vB s , which produce energy injection from the solar wind to the magnetosphere by reconnection. This injection causes the Dst or the SYM-H indices, which are a proxy of the ring current (RC) intensity, to reach large negative values during the main phase of a geomagnetic storm. The Dst then returns to quiet-time values during the recovery phase. Exponential or hyperbolic evolution has been proposed for this recovery phase, based on the DPS but neglecting the energy injection rate of energy, U I during this phase. However, during the passage of HSSs, the evolution of recovery departs from these profiles, lasting a longer time. The main contributor to a longer recovery period of CIR driven geomagnetic storms has been associated with the oscillatory IMF with southward turnings observed after the arrival of CIR in the upcoming solar wind (Tsurutani & Gonzalez, 1987). 

Figure 1 shows the geomagnetic storm starting on 23 April (DoY 113) 2023, due to an ICME, with a typical fast exponential recovery, and the storm starting on 19 May (DoY 139) 2023, due to an interaction region ahead of a HSS. This last storm exhibits a recovery phase far from an exponential profile. Even more, from DoY 140 at ∼20 UT to DoY 141 at ∼16 UT, a linear profile can be guessed in the SYM-H index evolution. 

Large-amplitude fluctuations in IMF components during the passage of a HSS have been identified as Alfvén waves (Alfvén, 1942;Belcher et al., 1969;Smith et al., 1995). CIR-driven disturbances often involve more turbulent and compressive interactions, which can enhance Alfvénic fluctuations, particularly in the outer Heliosphere and Heliosheath.

Title: Diagnostic study of geomagnetic storm-induced ionospheric changes over VLF signal propagation paths in mid-latitude D-region
Snippet: A CME is the impulsive release of solar material into interplanetary space from a solar active region that may, or may not, be associated with a solar flare (Youssef, 2012). Conversely, a CIR is the result of a high-speed stream (HSS) emitted from a solar coronal hole overtaking the background solar wind (Choi et al., 2009). In both cases the shock front at the leading edge of the interplanetary disturbance increases the ram pressure imposed on the dayside magnetopause causing a reconfiguration of the dayside Chapman-Ferraro current system (Chapman and Ferraro, 1930) and, in turn, the magnetosphere as a whole (Ganushkina et al., 2018). A typical geomagnetic storm has three phases consisting of 1) a sudden storm commencement (SSC) at the time of the increased ram pressure, 2) a main phase as the ring current is energized and 3) a recovery phase as the magnetosphere returns to a more quiescent ground state (Akasofu, 2018;Gonzalez et al., 1994). There are distinct differences between how and when CME-driven versus CIR-driven storms affect the earth (Borovsky and Denton, 2006). Typically, CME-driven storms are stronger, with regards to Dst (Tsurutani et al., 2006) and occur more frequently near the maximum in the sun's 11-year activity cycle (Gonzalez et al., 1999) whereas CIR-driven storms are weaker and occur predominantly on the decreasing phase of solar activity (Tsurutani et al., 1995). While the impacts of both CME and CIR-driven geomagnetic storms on the middle-to-upper atmosphere have been extensively studied and well known (Fuller-Rowell et al., 1994;Burch, 2016;Heelis and Maute, 2020), less certain are the geomagnetic storm effects in the lower ionosphere (Lastovicka, 1996;Kumar and Kumar, 2014).

Title: Properties of Ion Upflows in the Low‐Altitude Polar Ionosphere During CIR‐ and CME‐ Driven Magnetic Storms Based on Long‐Term EISCAT Observations
Snippet: The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.

Snippet: In this study, based on the Dynamic‐Kinetic Fluid (DyFK) model, we conduct simulations on the field‐aligned transport of cold ions (<1 eV) within three independent closed flux tubes from different starting points (L = 3.0 Re, L = 3.122 Re and L = 3.5 Re, respectively) during the 2015 St. Patrick's Day storm. These flux tubes magnetically connect the plasmaspheric plume with the ionospheric Storm Enhanced Density (SED) plume but drift toward the dayside magnetopause under E×B effects. Meanwhile, we can obtain the density variations of three ions species (H+, O+, and He+, respectively) around the flux tubes' apex (at the magnetic equator) as a function of the L shell. The simulations present the temporal evolution of cold plasma along these drifting flux tubes. We found that with increasing initial L shell location of the flux tube, there are more ionospheric cold light ions (H+ and He+) flowing into the equatorial region while the inflows of cold heavy ions (O+) toward the equator decrease. As the simulated flux tube drifts toward dayside magnetopause from the main plasmasphere (L = 3.0 Re), the SED sourced heavy ions pile up near the magnetic equator at low L shells (L < 4.0 Re) due to gravitational effects, while the light ions rapidly reach density equilibrium along the flux tube. With the flux tube drifting beyond L > 4.0 Re, the piled‐up cold heavy ions will later transport into the magnetic equatorial region and furnish the dayside magnetosphere, demonstrating that the SED is another supplier of magnetospheric cold heavy ions (O+).

Snippet: A noticeable difference is observed between dayside O + density profiles during CMEs (red) and CIRs (blue) disturbed orbits (Figure 9a). 

Ion density began to diverge above 240 km, with CIR profiles showing more than an order of magnitude decrease in the O + above 450 km compared to CMEs. Similar behavior is observed for the lighter ions C + , N + , and OH + on both the dayside (Figures 9e-g) and nightside (Figures 9l-n), with the nightside exhibiting a larger decrease in the density. However, the heavier ions (O2 + , CO2 + , & NO + ) show a much more pronounced decrease in density at all altitudes during the presence of CIRs as compared to CMEs, particularly on the nightside (Figures 9b-d and   Figures 9i-k). The difference between the nightside plasma density during CIRs and mean quiet-time profiles is ranging from one to two orders, whereas it is nearly one order during CMEs. 

The mean peak altitude of lighter ions is observed to be lesser during CIR and CME events as compared to mean quiet-time on both dayside and nightside. In addition, the mean peak altitude of lighter ions is observed to be lesser during CIR events as compared to CME events. The peak altitude and associated ion density with STDEV for both dayside and nightside profiles (CMEs vs CIRs) are listed in Table 2. On the dayside, the difference in the mean peak altitude (during CIRs) for O + , C + , N + , and OH + ranges from 5 to 30 km below that of observed during CMEs. On the nightside, this difference increases, ranging from 10 to 45 km below the peak altitude observed during CMEs.
</snippet>
