Title: Modeling of CME and CIR driven geomagnetic storms by means of artificial neural networks
Snippet: CIRs are believed to be an interplanetary origin of geomagnetic activity during the declining phase of the solar activity cycle (Richardson et al., 2000). 

Apart from the CMEs and CIRs solar origins, in what follows we consider both events as they manifest themselves as the solar wind disturbances at the libration point L1. CMEs at the libration point L1 can be recognized by sharp increase of particles density and speed. As magnetic field lines are frozen in the plasmoid, the temperature is decreasing and the IMF oscillates on timescale of days. The time distribution of geomagnetic disturbances according to their cause and intensity shows large variability in the course of solar cycle. CIRs are typically manifested by short increase of particle density and long (several days) increase of temperature and speed of the solar wind at the libration point L1. CIRs between fast and slow solar wind can thus periodically pass over the Earth and cause recurrent geomagnetic storms. 

Numerous studies show that CME and CIR events are different with characteristics specific to their type. The events due to CME tend to be shorter, more intense, with higher solar wind speeds. CMEs are responsible for greater changes in geomagnetic response and have very high values for energy input to geomagnetic storms. CIRs may not be as intense in their onset, but they are more efficient in their energy transfer to the magnetosphere. Within CIRs, the IMF presents a highly fluctuating southward component (Turner et al., 2006) and thus the geoeffectiveness of CIRs is usually weaker than those of CMEs. In Alves et al. (2006), the geoeffectiveness of CIRs was assessed during the solar wind observational period 1964-2003 and approximately one third of the CIR events observed near the Earth was found geoeffective. The contribution of CIRs and CMEs to geomagnetic activity during the 23rd solar cycle was assessed in Zhang et al. (2008). 

One of the most pronounced differences between CME and CIR driven geomagnetic storms is in their recovery phases (Laughlin et al., 2008).
</snippet>

Title: Distinctive response of thermospheric cooling to ICME and CIR-driven geomagnetic storms
Snippet: In order to understand the average trend of the thermospheric cooling and its response to energy input, we performed a superposed epoch analysis (SEA) study with zero epoch time corresponding to the storm's main phase. The SEA of the CME-and CIR-storms are, respectively, depicted in Figures 2A-E, A1-E1. The horizontal dotted lines represent the pre-onset value. It can clearly see that as the storm intensifies, the thermospheric density also increases both during the CME-and CIR-storms (Figures 2C, C1). The maximum density enhancement occurs within a day of onset, similar to the previous reported results (Lei et al., 2011;Chen et al., 2012;Chen et al., 2104;  and 0.28 mW m −2 for CIR-storm, respectively. This indicates that the impact of the ICME-driven storms is much more than the CIR-driven storms as far as the magnitude is concerned. However, it is interesting to note here that the cooling fluxes take more time (>6-7 days) to recover during CIR-driven storms, whereas, the recovery rate is faster (~3-4 days) for ICME-driven storms. 

In order to understand the impact of the energetic particle precipitations and the energy input from magnetosphere on the thermospheric cooling emission, Figure 3 is presented. Figures 3A-F, A1-F1, respectively, show the DMSP measured electron flux, ion flux along with the Epsilon (ε) and Newell coupling functions (CF) during CME-and CIR-storms. It can be seen that the particle (electron and ion) fluxes and the coupling functions show strong enhancement during both the storm periods. The enhancement in the particle fluxes and the CFs during CME-storm is higher than the CIR-storm. The εparameter shows higher enhancement as compared to the Newell's. The relative enhancement in ε-parameter is more than 50% and 30% during CME-and CIR-storm, respectively, as compared to the quiet value. Whereas, the Newell's CF undergoes enhancement of about 7% and 5%, respectively.

Sufficiency check and plan:

- Observational evidence of cumulative transport differences: main vs recovery contributions, with species dependence (H+, He+, O+).

Summary and definitions
Cold “ions” here refer to thermally distributed (non-rigidly ballistic) ions in the energy range from thermal up to a few 100–300 keV that are transported into and within the inner magnetosphere (L ~ 3–5 and near geostationary orbit) by convection, reconnection, and cross-field diffusion during storm-time activity. The question asks whether storms driven by corotating interaction regions (CIRs) produce different cumulative cold ion transport (H+, He+, O+) into the inner magnetosphere than those driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs), explicitly including both main-phase and recovery-phase contributions.

Mechanistic contrasts that shape cumulative transport
CIR- and CME-driven disturbances couple to the magnetosphere via similar reconnection-driven processes (southward IMF, prompt penetration), but they differ in duration, intensity, and substorm statistics, which modulate time-integrated transport. CME-driven storms are typically shorter, stronger (larger Dst), with a rapid main phase and a recovery that rebounds faster over days, whereas CIR-driven storms are recurrent with prolonged recovery that can last from several to many days due to oscillatory southward IMF and wave-driven convection behind the interaction region front. <cite id="7336f0c7-0">CIR-driven storms typically exhibit prolonged recovery phases that can extend from several days to multiple weeks, in contrast to CME-driven storms whose recovery phases are generally shorter (one to two days)</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-2">CME-driven storms are stronger and more frequent near solar maximum, whereas CIR-driven storms are weaker and recurrent in the declining phase; storm onsets differ (SSC for shocks vs gradual for HSS)</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-4">Superposed-epoch analyses show larger storm impacts and faster recovery (~3–4 days) during ICME/CME storms than CIR storms, whose recovery takes >6–7 days</cite>. These global differences translate into distinct storm-time convection histories and substorm activity chains that govern how cold ions are injected, circulate, and accumulate in the inner magnetosphere.

Observational signatures of cumulative transport by phase and driver
Storm-phase dependence within a driver:
- CIR-driven storm example across L ~ 3–5: During the main phase, H+ flux increases are localized to low energies (<60 keV), indicating efficient injection but limited immediate energization; in the recovery phase, high-energy H+ (>100 keV) fluxes can rise, implying continued energization and/or inward transport. Heavy ions (He+, O+) show opposite behavior—enhancements at both low and high energies during the main phase, evidencing effective entry and accumulation; thus, heavy-ion flux increases are stronger in the main phase, while H+ gains prominence into recovery. <cite id="c2a22051-0">During the main phase only low-energy H+ flux was enhanced in L ~ 3–5; during recovery high-energy H+ flux also increased; for He+ and O+, both low-energy and high-energy fluxes were enhanced during the main phase, indicating effective injection of high-energy heavy ions into the inner magnetosphere</cite>.
- Ion upflows and precipitation: Nightside ion upflows persist for ~3 days after onset for CIR storms versus ~1 day and more intense but bursty for CME storms; upflow-driven transport and precipitation deliver cold ions into the inner magnetosphere rapidly at the start of CME storms and over multiple days after onset for CIR storms. <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CIR-driven storms produced ion upflows continuing 3 days after onset (Tromsø), whereas CME-driven storms showed a sudden, intense, and rapid (∼1 day) upflow response; CMEs exhibit stronger, more concentrated precipitation early on, while CIRs show successive substorms and longer-lasting upflows</cite>.

Across drivers and phases (superposed epoch):
- Ion temperature evolution and energy coupling: CME-driven storms heat ions rapidly at onset and cool during the main phase, with recovery warming; CIR-driven storms warm during recovery, implying different cumulative energy/flux histories for inner-magnetosphere populations. <cite id="7336f0c7-1">Keesee et al. (2014) found ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while for CME storms temperature rose rapidly at onset and cooled off during the main phase</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-1">Same superposed-epoch analysis shows distinct ion temperature evolutions by driver</cite>.
- Thermospheric/energetic coupling proxies: For ICME/CME storms, density and cooling fluxes rise sharply and recover faster (~3–4 days), indicating stronger and shorter energy input; CIR storms show slower enhancement and longer recovery (>6–7 days) with stronger correlations/lag of ions and electrons to magnetospheric inputs, consistent with gradual, extended cold plasma loading and transport. <cite id="9d725e89-0">Thermospheric cooling fluxes increase quickly with faster recovery (~3–4 days) during CME storms, while CIR storms show slower enhancement and longer recovery (>6–7 days)</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-4">CME-driven storms produce larger density enhancements and faster recovery than CIR-driven storms; particle fluxes and coupling functions peak higher in CMEs</cite>. Although these are not purely “cold ion” measurements, they capture the cumulative effects of ion and electron precipitation and entry into the upper atmosphere and magnetosphere that directly replenish cold ion populations.

Species-resolved transport pathways and phase dependence:
- SED-to-magnetosphere coupling: During storms, enhanced ionospheric plasma (Storm-Enhanced Density, SED) drives cold H+ and He+ inflows into dayside equatorial regions in the main phase, with light ions equilibrating rapidly and heavy ions piling up near the equator at low L-shells due to gravity, later leaking inward during recovery; this mechanism supplies both light and heavy cold ions but favors light-ion equatorial access and heavy-ion accumulation that can migrate into the inner magnetosphere during recovery. <cite id="c2a22051-2">Simulations show more cold H+ and He+ flowing into equatorial regions from SED-sourced plumes as flux tubes drift dayside, with O+ inflows reduced toward equator due to gravitational focusing; heavy ions pile up near equator at L < 4 and later transport inward</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-3">Increasing initial L-shell enhances inflow of cold H+ and He+, while O+ inflow decreases; heavy ions pile up near equator and later furnish the dayside magnetosphere</cite>.
- Charge-state dependence in recovery: Near-Earth magnetotail observations show preferential energization/heating of lower-charge-state heavier ions (He+) at lower energies during the main phase, with enhanced He+ flux at decreasing energies; the mechanism and dominant supply source (ionospheric vs solar wind) depend on phase and L, and remain nuanced during recovery. <cite id="c2a22051-4">He+/He++ and He+/H+ energy-density ratios increase at lower energies during the main phase, consistent with enhanced He+ supply from the ionosphere; the dominant process and supply source depend on phase and L-shell</cite>.
- Dayside-to-tail coupling: Dawn–dusk–aligned transport demonstrates how reconnection and global convection move solar-wind-origin ions into closed-field regions, with He2+ distributions shaped by E×B drift and gradient/curvature drifts; this illustrates efficient cold ion circulation that can contribute to inner-magnetosphere filling during both phases. <cite id="c2a22051-1">Magnetic reconnection transports solar-wind ions into closed flux tubes, with He2+ >~10 keV showing dawn–dusk asymmetric distributions set by convection and drifts</cite>.

Putting phases together: cumulative differences between CIR and CME drivers
- Magnitude and duration: Because CME-driven storms inject more energy more quickly and then decay faster, their cumulative storm-time (main+recovery) transport of both thermal and suprathermal ions into the inner magnetosphere tends to be larger and more concentrated within ~1–2 days. In contrast, CIR-driven storms deliver a larger time-integrated but more diffuse loading sustained over ~5–7+ days, favoring extended recovery-phase transport and heavier reliance on substorm-generated, cold plasma convection. <cite id="9d725e89-4">CME-driven storms show larger density and flux enhancements and faster recovery than CIR-driven storms</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-0">CIR-driven storms have prolonged recovery (several days to weeks) with oscillatory southward IMF sustaining convection</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CIR-driven storms feature multi-day ion upflows and successive substorms during recovery, whereas CME-driven storms concentrate upflows and precipitation within one day</cite>.
- Phase-resolved transport into inner magnetosphere:
  • CIR vs CME main phases: CIR main phases enhance heavy-ion (He+, O+) fluxes strongly at low and high energies, evidencing efficient entry and energization; H+ increases are mainly low-energy. CME main phases are characterized by rapid onset convection and strong bursty precipitation, with H+ fluxes elevated at low energies and heavy-ion enhancements that depend on the balance of ionospheric and solar-wind sources; however, the prompt, intense nature of CMEs implies steeper early-time flux rises that can dominate instantaneous inner-magnetosphere filling. <cite id="c2a22051-0">CIR main-phase heavy-ion flux enhancements at multiple energies; H+ mainly low-energy</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CME-driven storms produce strong, concentrated precipitation during the first day</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-4">He+ preferential energization at lower energies during main phase suggests ionospheric dominance</cite>.
  • Recovery phases: CIR-driven storms show multi-day upflows and substorm chains that sustain cold ion transport into the inner magnetosphere, with evidence of increased high-energy H+ and continued heavy-ion circulation; in thermospheric cooling diagnostics, CIRs show slower decay implying prolonged cumulative energy input. CME-driven storms exhibit rapid recovery, with inner-magnetosphere signatures cooling faster and returning toward quiet values within ~3–4 days. <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CIR-driven storms maintain ion upflows for ~3 days and show successive substorms in recovery</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-0">CIR recovery-phase increase of high-energy H+ flux</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-0">Thermospheric cooling fluxes recover in ~3–4 days for CMEs but >6–7 days for CIRs</cite>.
- Species differences: Cold H+ is efficiently transported into the inner magnetosphere during both CIR and CME main phases, but CIR-driven conditions favor longer-lived recovery-phase H+ energization via substorm-driven upflows and SED coupling. Heavy ions (He+, O+) show stronger main-phase enhancements during CIR-driven storms, with modeled accumulation near equator and inward leakage during recovery; CME-driven storms can also enhance He+ at low energies through ionospheric supply, but their short duration produces less cumulative heavy-ion transport over main+recovery. <cite id="c2a22051-0">CIR main-phase enhancements for He+ and O+ at both low and high energies</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-2">SED-driven cold H+ and He+ inflow into equatorial regions during main phase, with O+ pile-up near equator feeding inward during recovery</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-4">He+ preferential energization at low energies during main phase consistent with ionospheric supply</cite>.

Bottom line: Do cumulative cold ion transports differ?
Yes. When integrating over both main and recovery phases, CME-driven storms tend to deliver larger, more rapid, and more concentrated cumulative cold ion transport into the inner magnetosphere—dominant in the first ~1–2 days—due to their higher-intensity, shorter-duration convection and precipitation. CIR-driven storms, by contrast, produce smaller-magnitude but longer-duration cumulative transport sustained over 5–7+ days, with stronger heavy-ion (He+, O+) enhancements during the main phase and continued H+ and heavy-ion transport during recovery via substorm chains and SED-driven convection; thus, the CIR-driven cumulative profile is broader and more prolonged, especially favoring inner-magnetosphere penetration of heavy ions during main phase and sustained H+-rich replenishment during recovery. <cite id="9d725e89-4">CME-driven storms produce larger density/flux enhancements and faster recovery than CIR-driven storms, indicating more intense short-term cumulative transport</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-0">CIR-driven storms feature prolonged recovery due to persistent southward IMF and Alfvenic fluctuations</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CIR-driven storms show multi-day ion upflows and successive substorms, sustaining inner-magnetosphere transport</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-0">Heavy-ion (He+, O+) flux increases are stronger during CIR main phases, with H+ high-energy increases in recovery</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-2">SED-to-dayside magnetosphere transport enhances cold H+ and He+ during main phase and furnishes O+ later via gravity-assisted inward leakage</cite>.

Uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Quantitative head-to-head integrals: Most inner-magnetosphere flux measurements are event-specific; multi-storm superposed-epoch, species-resolved H+/He+/O+ flux integrals at L ~ 3–5 or geostationary orbit stratified by CIR vs CME would reduce uncertainty. <cite id="7336f0c7-1">Keesee et al. (2014) provide driver-stratified superposed-epoch evolutions</cite> <cite id="9d725e89-4">SEA across CME and CIR shows stronger/more rapid CME impacts</cite>, but species-specific cumulative transport across many storms remains sparse.
- Source attribution: The balance of solar-wind-origin vs ionospheric-origin ions during each phase affects cumulative transport; distinguishing these sources in situ (e.g., oxygen isotopes for solar wind vs ionospheric origin) and via global models would refine comparisons. <cite id="c2a22051-4">Evidence points to ionospheric dominance during main/early recovery for storms, with He+ preferential energization</cite>.
- Cold-ion vs energetic-particle separation: Thermospheric cooling and ring-current proxies respond to both cold ions and energetic particles; complementary cold-ion-only measurements (e.g., lower-energy channels, O+ identification) and modeling that isolates Fokker–Planck transport would better isolate “cold ion” transport. <cite id="c2a22051-0">Observed flux changes at low magnetic moments isolate cold H+ enhancements</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-1">He2+ distributions demonstrate reconnection-driven transport of solar-wind-origin ions into closed flux tubes</cite>.

Practical implications
For space environment forecasting, treat CME-driven storms as high-flux, short-duration cold-ion injection events primarily affecting L > 4–5 during main phase and rapidly clearing in recovery, whereas CIR-driven storms warrant accounting for multi-day cumulative transport with stronger inner-magnetosphere heavy-ion loading during main phase and prolonged H+ replenishment into recovery via substorm-driven upflows and SED coupling. <cite id="9d725e89-0">CME storms: quick, strong enhancements and faster recovery (~3–4 days)</cite> <cite id="7336f0c7-3">CIR storms: multi-day upflows and substorms sustaining transport</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-0">CIR: heavy-ion main-phase increases; H+ high-energy increases in recovery</cite> <cite id="c2a22051-2">SED-driven cold-ion inflows into dayside magnetosphere during main phase, furnishing O+ later</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Alfvénic Contribution From the Solar Wind to Magnetospheric Dynamics
Snippet: CIR-driven storms typically exhibit prolonged recovery phases that can extend from several days to multiple weeks, as noted by Borovsky and Denton (2006); Tsurutani et al. (2006). In contrast, the recovery phases associated with CME-driven storms are generally shorter, often lasting only one to 2 days (Zhang et al., 2007). 

Both ICMEs and HSSs include among their signatures large values of vB s , which produce energy injection from the solar wind to the magnetosphere by reconnection. This injection causes the Dst or the SYM-H indices, which are a proxy of the ring current (RC) intensity, to reach large negative values during the main phase of a geomagnetic storm. The Dst then returns to quiet-time values during the recovery phase. Exponential or hyperbolic evolution has been proposed for this recovery phase, based on the DPS but neglecting the energy injection rate of energy, U I during this phase. However, during the passage of HSSs, the evolution of recovery departs from these profiles, lasting a longer time. The main contributor to a longer recovery period of CIR driven geomagnetic storms has been associated with the oscillatory IMF with southward turnings observed after the arrival of CIR in the upcoming solar wind (Tsurutani & Gonzalez, 1987). 

Figure 1 shows the geomagnetic storm starting on 23 April (DoY 113) 2023, due to an ICME, with a typical fast exponential recovery, and the storm starting on 19 May (DoY 139) 2023, due to an interaction region ahead of a HSS. This last storm exhibits a recovery phase far from an exponential profile. Even more, from DoY 140 at ∼20 UT to DoY 141 at ∼16 UT, a linear profile can be guessed in the SYM-H index evolution. 

Large-amplitude fluctuations in IMF components during the passage of a HSS have been identified as Alfvén waves (Alfvén, 1942;Belcher et al., 1969;Smith et al., 1995). CIR-driven disturbances often involve more turbulent and compressive interactions, which can enhance Alfvénic fluctuations, particularly in the outer Heliosphere and Heliosheath.

Title: Short-term variability of the Sun-Earth system: an overview of progress made during the CAWSES-II period
Snippet: Keesee et al. (2014) performed superposed epoch analysis of 21 CME-driven and 15 CIR-driven storms during the June 2008 to April 2012 time frame and different evolutions of the ion temperature: the ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while it increased rapidly at the onset of CME storms and cooled off during the main phase. Borovsky and Denton (2013) compared CIR storms associated with helmet streamers and pseudo-streamers. They found that pseudo-streamer CIR storms tend not to have a calm (Tsurutani et al. 1995) before the storm, with weaker superdense plasma sheet and electron radiation belt dropout.

Title: Diagnostic study of geomagnetic storm-induced ionospheric changes over VLF signal propagation paths in mid-latitude D-region
Snippet: A CME is the impulsive release of solar material into interplanetary space from a solar active region that may, or may not, be associated with a solar flare (Youssef, 2012). Conversely, a CIR is the result of a high-speed stream (HSS) emitted from a solar coronal hole overtaking the background solar wind (Choi et al., 2009). In both cases the shock front at the leading edge of the interplanetary disturbance increases the ram pressure imposed on the dayside magnetopause causing a reconfiguration of the dayside Chapman-Ferraro current system (Chapman and Ferraro, 1930) and, in turn, the magnetosphere as a whole (Ganushkina et al., 2018). A typical geomagnetic storm has three phases consisting of 1) a sudden storm commencement (SSC) at the time of the increased ram pressure, 2) a main phase as the ring current is energized and 3) a recovery phase as the magnetosphere returns to a more quiescent ground state (Akasofu, 2018;Gonzalez et al., 1994). There are distinct differences between how and when CME-driven versus CIR-driven storms affect the earth (Borovsky and Denton, 2006). Typically, CME-driven storms are stronger, with regards to Dst (Tsurutani et al., 2006) and occur more frequently near the maximum in the sun's 11-year activity cycle (Gonzalez et al., 1999) whereas CIR-driven storms are weaker and occur predominantly on the decreasing phase of solar activity (Tsurutani et al., 1995). While the impacts of both CME and CIR-driven geomagnetic storms on the middle-to-upper atmosphere have been extensively studied and well known (Fuller-Rowell et al., 1994;Burch, 2016;Heelis and Maute, 2020), less certain are the geomagnetic storm effects in the lower ionosphere (Lastovicka, 1996;Kumar and Kumar, 2014).

Title: Properties of Ion Upflows in the Low‐Altitude Polar Ionosphere During CIR‐ and CME‐ Driven Magnetic Storms Based on Long‐Term EISCAT Observations
Snippet: The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.

Title: Effects of CME and CIR induced geomagnetic storms on low-latitude ionization over Indian longitudes in terms of neutral dynamics
Snippet: CME-driven storms are dominant at solar maximum while the CIR-driven storms tend to occur during the declining phase of a solar cycle. Occurrence pattern of the CMEdriven storms is irregular, with highest occurrence frequency during solar maximum whereas CIR-driven storms repeat with a period of about 27 days as a result of Sun's rotation, mainly during a solar cycle's declining phase. 

Furthermore, CME-driven storms have a shorter recovery phase lasting for about 12 days while the CIR-driven storms have a prolonged recovery phase that can last for several days. Storm Sudden Commencements (SSC) are associated with the interplanetary shocks driven by the CMEs while the gradual onsets are driven by HSSW streams (Borovsky and Denton, 2006). 

The beginning of geomagnetic disturbances is associated with large variations of the IMF Bz and Prompt Penetration Electric Fields (PPEF) which results from the transmission of magnetospheric convection electric field from high to low latitudes (Vasyliunas, 1970). The equivalent current system which is associated with the prompt penetration (Nishida, 1968a) has average periods of the order of few minutes to 3 hours. During the previous decades, both theoretical and experimental studies have clearly highlighted the characteristics of prompt penetration of magnetospheric convection electric field from high to low latitudes and the severe effects on low latitude electrodynamics (Fejer et al., 1983;Spiro et al., 1988;Fejer and Scherliess, 1997;Basu et al., 2010). 

At the higher latitudes, Auroral Electrojet (AE) currents transfer energy in the form of heat, by the physical process of Joule heating, to the neutral gas. This Joule heating is given by the power per unit volume dP/dV = J.E, (where J is the electric current and E the electric field). Additionally, by the process of Ampere force given by cross product of J and B, where B is the magnetic field, AE currents move the neutral wind by transfer of momentum.

snippet.text: A CME is the impulsive release of solar material into interplanetary space from a solar active region that may, or may not, be associated with a solar flare (Youssef, 2012). Conversely, a CIR is the result of a high-speed stream (HSS) emitted from a solar coronal hole overtaking the background solar wind (Choi et al., 2009). In both cases the shock front at the leading edge of the interplanetary disturbance increases the ram pressure imposed on the dayside magnetopause causing a reconfiguration of the dayside Chapman-Ferraro current system (Chapman and Ferraro, 1930) and, in turn, the magnetosphere as a whole (Ganushkina et al., 2018). A typical geomagnetic storm has three phases consisting of 1) a sudden storm commencement (SSC) at the time of the increased ram pressure, 2) a main phase as the ring current is energized and 3) a recovery phase as the magnetosphere returns to a more quiescent ground state (Akasofu, 2018;Gonzalez et al., 1994). There are distinct differences between how and when CME-driven versus CIR-driven storms affect the earth (Borovsky and Denton, 2006). Typically, CME-driven storms are stronger, with regards to Dst (Tsurutani et al., 2006) and occur more frequently near the maximum in the sun's 11-year activity cycle (Gonzalez et al., 1999) whereas CIR-driven storms are weaker and occur predominantly on the decreasing phase of solar activity (Tsurutani et al., 1995). While the impacts of both CME and CIR-driven geomagnetic storms on the middle-to-upper atmosphere have been extensively studied and well known (Fuller-Rowell et al., 1994;Burch, 2016;Heelis and Maute, 2020), less certain are the geomagnetic storm effects in the lower ionosphere (Lastovicka, 1996;Kumar and Kumar, 2014).

snippet.text:
The differences in the duration of ion upflows between CIR-and CME-driven storms are remarkable on the nightside at Tromsø. To minimize the influence of the Dst index, CIR-driven large storms must be compared to CME-driven small storms at Tromsø, as mentioned by Ogawa et al. (2019). The ion upflows continued for 3 days after storm onset during the CIR-driven storms, whereas the upward velocity suddenly increased and rapidly decreased within one day during the CME-driven storms (see Figures 2 and 3). The upward velocity and flux were strongly enhanced on the first day of the storm during CME-driven storms. These upflows were triggered by precipitation on the nightside (see Table 4). Thus, it is considered that the strong and concentrated precipitation occurred during CME-driven storms. Bursty and strong auroral emissions have been reported to be more pronounced during CME-driven storms than during CIR-driven storms (Borovsky & Denton, 2006). These phenomenological differences can be explained by the different characteristics of solar wind drivers, that is, CIRs and CMEs. As Kataoka and Miyoshi (2006) summarized, CIR storms are characterized by successive substorm activities during the recovery phase owing to an Alfven wave chain in the solar wind after the CIR passage. In contrast, the recovery phase of CME storms is characterized by a relatively rapid recovery and fewer substorm activities. 

On the other hand, frictional heating mainly caused ion upflows during both CIR-driven and CME-driven large storms, and did not cause them during small storms on the nightside at Tromsø. This indicates that frictional heating is closely related to the Dst index. Large storms can cause strong magnetospheric convection, resulting in strong ring currents, enhanced electric fields in the ionosphere, and auroral oval expansion.

snippet.text:
CME-driven storms are dominant at solar maximum while the CIR-driven storms tend to occur during the declining phase of a solar cycle. Occurrence pattern of the CMEdriven storms is irregular, with highest occurrence frequency during solar maximum whereas CIR-driven storms repeat with a period of about 27 days as a result of Sun's rotation, mainly during a solar cycle's declining phase. 

Furthermore, CME-driven storms have a shorter recovery phase lasting for about 12 days while the CIR-driven storms have a prolonged recovery phase that can last for several days. Storm Sudden Commencements (SSC) are associated with the interplanetary shocks driven by the CMEs while the gradual onsets are driven by HSSW streams (Borovsky and Denton, 2006). 

The beginning of geomagnetic disturbances is associated with large variations of the IMF Bz and Prompt Penetration Electric Fields (PPEF) which results from the transmission of magnetospheric convection electric field from high to low latitudes (Vasyliunas, 1970). The equivalent current system which is associated with the prompt penetration (Nishida, 1968a) has average periods of the order of few minutes to 3 hours. During the previous decades, both theoretical and experimental studies have clearly highlighted the characteristics of prompt penetration of magnetospheric convection electric field from high to low latitudes and the severe effects on low latitude electrodynamics (Fejer et al., 1983;Spiro et al., 1988;Fejer and Scherliess, 1997;Basu et al., 2010). 

At the higher latitudes, Auroral Electrojet (AE) currents transfer energy in the form of heat, by the physical process of Joule heating, to the neutral gas. This Joule heating is given by the power per unit volume dP/dV = J.E, (where J is the electric current and E the electric field). Additionally, by the process of Ampere force given by cross product of J and B, where B is the magnetic field, AE currents move the neutral wind by transfer of momentum.

documents.title: Alfvénic Contribution From the Solar Wind to Magnetospheric Dynamics
documents.snippet:
CIR-driven storms typically exhibit prolonged recovery phases that can extend from several days to multiple weeks, as noted by Borovsky and Denton (2006); Tsurutani et al. (2006). In contrast, the recovery phases associated with CME-driven storms are generally shorter, often lasting only one to 2 days (Zhang et al., 2007). 

Both ICMEs and HSSs include among their signatures large values of vB s , which produce energy injection from the solar wind to the magnetosphere by reconnection. This injection causes the Dst or the SYM-H indices, which are a proxy of the ring current (RC) intensity, to reach large negative values during the main phase of a geomagnetic storm. The Dst then returns to quiet-time values during the recovery phase. Exponential or hyperbolic evolution has been proposed for this recovery phase, based on the DPS but neglecting the energy injection rate of energy, U I during this phase. However, during the passage of HSSs, the evolution of recovery departs from these profiles, lasting a longer time. The main contributor to a longer recovery period of CIR driven geomagnetic storms has been associated with the oscillatory IMF with southward turnings observed after the arrival of CIR in the upcoming solar wind (Tsurutani & Gonzalez, 1987). 

Figure 1 shows the geomagnetic storm starting on 23 April (DoY 113) 2023, due to an ICME, with a typical fast exponential recovery, and the storm starting on 19 May (DoY 139) 2023, due to an interaction region ahead of a HSS. This last storm exhibits a recovery phase far from an exponential profile. Even more, from DoY 140 at ∼20 UT to DoY 141 at ∼16 UT, a linear profile can be guessed in the SYM-H index evolution. 

Large-amplitude fluctuations in IMF components during the passage of a HSS have been identified as Alfvén waves (Alfvén, 1942;Belcher et al., 1969;Smith et al., 1995). CIR-driven disturbances often involve more turbulent and compressive interactions, which can enhance Alfvénic fluctuations, particularly in the outer Heliosphere and Heliosheath.

Title: Evolutions of equatorial ring current ions during a magnetic storm
Snippet: The solar wind dynamic pressure gradually increases to ~7 nPa, leading to the excitation of ULF waves, as shown below. These solar wind conditions meet the characteristics of a corotating interaction region-driven (CIR-driven) storm (e.g., Borovsky and Denton, 2006;Kamide et al., 1998). The next three flux panels show the omnidirectional flux of hydrogen ions, helium ions, and oxygen ions, respectively. The three black solid lines on each flux panel mark the magnetic moments of 0.3, 0.6, and 1.2 keV/nT, respectively. The actual calculation is for 0.1, 0.2, …, 2.0 keV/nT ions with intervals of 0.1 keV/nT. Panels (h) and (i) show the electron number density N e and satellite's position given the McIlwain-L value. Here we focus on Orbits 3684 in L ~ 3-5 (the initial phase) and 3685 in L ~ 3-5 (the main phase). For convenience, the pink dotted line interval is replaced with the orbit number. As shown in Figure 1e, during the main phase (Orbit 3685 in L ~ 3-5), only low-energy (<60 keV) hydrogen ion flux was enhanced in the inner magnetosphere. During the recovery phase (Orbit 3686 in L ~ 3-5), the flux of high-energy (>100 keV) hydrogen ions also was enhanced. In contrast, as shown in Figures 1(f-g), the fluxes of both low-energy (<150 keV) and high-energy (>150 keV) heavy ions (He + , O + ) were enhanced in the inner magnetosphere during the main phase (Orbit 3685 in L ~ 3-5). The difference in behavior between heavy ions (He + , O + ) and hydrogen ions (H + ) in the main phase indicates that high-energy heavy ions can be effectively injected into the inner magnetosphere.

Title: Dawn/dusk asymmetry in particles of solar wind origin within the magnetosphere
Snippet: This covers the region where He 2+ ions are found in Figs. 6a-d, but we do not see any major distinction between this LLBL location and the auroral oval in general in Fig. 6, and some of it extends into the region that we have characterised as cusp. 

This result illustrates how magnetic reconnection and the associated global convection cycle is able to transport solar wind ions accessing the magnetosphere on open field lines and then subsequently circulate and energise them on closed field lines. In particular, it demonstrates that the distribution of He 2+ ions with energies greater than ∼10 keV at high invariant latitudes is dominated by ions drifting sunward in the magnetotail and that dawn-dusk asymmetry results from the combined effect of the convection electric field and gradient/curvature drifts.

Title: Simulation of Cold Ion Transport Originating From the SED Plume Into Dayside Magnetosphere
Snippet: In this study, based on the Dynamic‐Kinetic Fluid (DyFK) model, we conduct simulations on the field‐aligned transport of cold ions (<1 eV) within three independent closed flux tubes from different starting points (L = 3.0 Re, L = 3.122 Re and L = 3.5 Re, respectively) during the 2015 St. Patrick's Day storm. These flux tubes magnetically connect the plasmaspheric plume with the ionospheric Storm Enhanced Density (SED) plume but drift toward the dayside magnetopause under E×B effects. Meanwhile, we can obtain the density variations of three ions species (H+, O+, and He+, respectively) around the flux tubes' apex (at the magnetic equator) as a function of the L shell. The simulations present the temporal evolution of cold plasma along these drifting flux tubes. We found that with increasing initial L shell location of the flux tube, there are more ionospheric cold light ions (H+ and He+) flowing into the equatorial region while the inflows of cold heavy ions (O+) toward the equator decrease. As the simulated flux tube drifts toward dayside magnetopause from the main plasmasphere (L = 3.0 Re), the SED sourced heavy ions pile up near the magnetic equator at low L shells (L < 4.0 Re) due to gravitational effects, while the light ions rapidly reach density equilibrium along the flux tube. With the flux tube drifting beyond L > 4.0 Re, the piled‐up cold heavy ions will later transport into the magnetic equatorial region and furnish the dayside magnetosphere, demonstrating that the SED is another supplier of magnetospheric cold heavy ions (O+).

Title: Preferential Energization of Lower‐Charge‐State Heavier Ions in the Near‐Earth Magnetotail
Snippet: We believe that, at least during the main phase examined in this study, preferential heating and effective transport is the most plausible scenario, because ionospheric ions dominate over the solar wind ions during the main phase (Glocer et al., 2020;Kistler, 2020). During the recovery phase and quiet times, however, observations over a wide range of L and detailed analysis of substorm/non-substorm periods are needed to determine the dominant/most important process. 

The energy density observed by MEP-i showed an increase of the energy density ratios He+/He++ and He+/H+ at lower energies (Result 5), particularly for the May 2017 storm. At least two scenarios are possible to explain this feature. One is that He+ was supplied in a relatively larger amount at low energies compared with O+. The energy spectra showed that the He+ flux increased with decreasing energy, while the O+ flux remained at the same level. Another scenario is a decrease in ions of solar wind origin due to low solar wind density or less efficient entry. As several recent studies concluded that magnetospheric plasma is predominantly of ionospheric origin during magnetic storms (Glocer et al., 2020), particularly the main and early recovery phases (Kistler, 2020), it is likely that the He+/He++ and He+/H+ increases result from enhanced supply of He+.

Here we focus on Orbits 3684 in L ~ 3-5 (the initial phase) and 3685 in L ~ 3-5 (the main phase). For convenience, the pink dotted line interval is replaced with the orbit number. This covers the region where He 2+ ions are found in Figs. 6a-d, but we do not see any major distinction between this LLBL location and the auroral oval in general in Fig. 6, and some of it extends into the region that we have characterised as cusp. 

This result illustrates how magnetic reconnection and the associated global convection cycle is able to transport solar wind ions accessing the magnetosphere on open field lines and then subsequently circulate and energise them on closed field lines. In particular, it demonstrates that the distribution of He 2+ ions with energies greater than ∼10 keV at high invariant latitudes is dominated by ions drifting sunward in the magnetotail and that dawn-dusk asymmetry results from the combined effect of the convection electric field and gradient/curvature drifts.

documents.title: Simulation of Cold Ion Transport Originating From the SED Plume Into Dayside Magnetosphere
documents.snippet: In this study, based on the Dynamic‐Kinetic Fluid (DyFK) model, we conduct simulations on the field‐aligned transport of cold ions (<1 eV) within three independent closed flux tubes from different starting points (L = 3.0 Re, L = 3.122 Re and L = 3.5 Re, respectively) during the 2015 St. Patrick's Day storm. These flux tubes magnetically connect the plasmaspheric plume with the ionospheric Storm Enhanced Density (SED) plume but drift toward the dayside magnetopause under E×B effects. Meanwhile, we can obtain the density variations of three ions species (H+, O+, and He+, respectively) around the flux tubes' apex (at the magnetic equator) as a function of the L shell. The simulations present the temporal evolution of cold plasma along these drifting flux tubes. We found that with increasing initial L shell location of the flux tube, there are more ionospheric cold light ions (H+ and He+) flowing into the equatorial region while the inflows of cold heavy ions (O+) toward the equator decrease. As the simulated flux tube drifts toward dayside magnetopause from the main plasmasphere (L = 3.0 Re), the SED sourced heavy ions pile up near the magnetic equator at low L shells (L < 4.0 Re) due to gravitational effects, while the light ions rapidly reach density equilibrium along the flux tube. With the flux tube drifting beyond L > 4.0 Re, the piled‐up cold heavy ions will later transport into the magnetic equatorial region and furnish the dayside magnetosphere, demonstrating that the SED is another supplier of magnetospheric cold heavy ions (O+).

documents.title: Preferential Energization of Lower‐Charge‐State Heavier Ions in the Near‐Earth Magnetotail
documents.snippet:
We believe that, at least during the main phase examined in this study, preferential heating and effective transport is the most plausible scenario, because ionospheric ions dominate over the solar wind ions during the main phase (Glocer et al., 2020;Kistler, 2020). During the recovery phase and quiet times, however, observations over a wide range of L and detailed analysis of substorm/non-substorm periods are needed to determine the dominant/most important process. 

The energy density observed by MEP-i showed an increase of the energy density ratios He+/He++ and He+/H+ at lower energies (Result 5), particularly for the May 2017 storm. At least two scenarios are possible to explain this feature. One is that He+ was supplied in a relatively larger amount at low energies compared with O+. The energy spectra showed that the He+ flux increased with decreasing energy, while the O+ flux remained at the same level. Another scenario is a decrease in ions of solar wind origin due to low solar wind density or less efficient entry. As several recent studies concluded that magnetospheric plasma is predominantly of ionospheric origin during magnetic storms (Glocer et al., 2020), particularly the main and early recovery phases (Kistler, 2020), it is likely that the He+/He++ and He+/H+ increases result from enhanced supply of He+.

Title: Distinctive response of thermospheric cooling to ICME and CIR-driven geomagnetic storms
Snippet: We performed superposed epoch analysis and detailed crosscorrelation study to investigate the response of CO 2 15 μm and NO 5.3 μm cooling emissions during ICME-and CIR-driven storms by utilizing the data from TIMED-SABER satellite along with other datasets. The silent features emerged from this investigation are as follows: (I) The thermospheric cooling fluxes undergo quick and strong enhancement with a faster recovery (~3-4 days) during CME storms. Whereas, a slower enhancement and a longer recovery (>6-7 days) is observed during CIR. (II) The Akasofu and Newell coupling functions display different behavior during CMEand CIR-storms. (III) The NO cooling flux during CIR storm shows longer time-lag with all parameters than the CME-event. (IV) The ions (>0.945 keV) and electrons (>9.45 keV) display a stronger correlation and higher timelag during CIR storms for NO cooling emission. The different behavior of NO cooling emission during ICME and CIRdriven storms could be due to the impacts of the both proton and electron fluxes.

Title: Short-term variability of the Sun-Earth system: an overview of progress made during the CAWSES-II period
Snippet: Keesee et al. (2014) performed superposed epoch analysis of 21 CME-driven and 15 CIR-driven storms during the June 2008 to April 2012 time frame and different evolutions of the ion temperature: the ion temperature increased in the recovery phase of CIR storms, while it increased rapidly at the onset of CME storms and cooled off during the main phase. Borovsky and Denton (2013) compared CIR storms associated with helmet streamers and pseudo-streamers. They found that pseudo-streamer CIR storms tend not to have a calm (Tsurutani et al. 1995) before the storm, with weaker superdense plasma sheet and electron radiation belt dropout.

Title: A Comparison of the Impacts of CMEs and CIRs on the Martian Dayside and Nightside Ionospheric Species
Snippet: A noticeable difference is observed between dayside O + density profiles during CMEs (red) and CIRs (blue) disturbed orbits (Figure 9a). 

Ion density began to diverge above 240 km, with CIR profiles showing more than an order of magnitude decrease in the O + above 450 km compared to CMEs. Similar behavior is observed for the lighter ions C + , N + , and OH + on both the dayside (Figures 9e-g) and nightside (Figures 9l-n), with the nightside exhibiting a larger decrease in the density. However, the heavier ions (O2 + , CO2 + , & NO + ) show a much more pronounced decrease in density at all altitudes during the presence of CIRs as compared to CMEs, particularly on the nightside (Figures 9b-d and   Figures 9i-k). The difference between the nightside plasma density during CIRs and mean quiet-time profiles is ranging from one to two orders, whereas it is nearly one order during CMEs. 

The mean peak altitude of lighter ions is observed to be lesser during CIR and CME events as compared to mean quiet-time on both dayside and nightside. In addition, the mean peak altitude of lighter ions is observed to be lesser during CIR events as compared to CME events. The peak altitude and associated ion density with STDEV for both dayside and nightside profiles (CMEs vs CIRs) are listed in Table 2. On the dayside, the difference in the mean peak altitude (during CIRs) for O + , C + , N + , and OH + ranges from 5 to 30 km below that of observed during CMEs. On the nightside, this difference increases, ranging from 10 to 45 km below the peak altitude observed during CMEs.

Title: Modeling of CME and CIR driven geomagnetic storms by means of artificial neural networks
Snippet: CIRs are believed to be an interplanetary origin of geomagnetic activity during the declining phase of the solar activity cycle (Richardson et al., 2000). 

Apart from the CMEs and CIRs solar origins, in what follows we consider both events as they manifest themselves as the solar wind disturbances at the libration point L1. CMEs at the libration point L1 can be recognized by sharp increase of particles density and speed. As magnetic field lines are frozen in the plasmoid, the temperature is decreasing and the IMF oscillates on timescale of days. The time distribution of geomagnetic disturbances according to their cause and intensity shows large variability in the course of solar cycle. CIRs are typically manifested by short increase of particle density and long (several days) increase of temperature and speed of the solar wind at the libration point L1. CIRs between fast and slow solar wind can thus periodically pass over the Earth and cause recurrent geomagnetic storms. 

Numerous studies show that CME and CIR events are different with characteristics specific to their type. The events due to CME tend to be shorter, more intense, with higher solar wind speeds. CMEs are responsible for greater changes in geomagnetic response and have very high values for energy input to geomagnetic storms. CIRs may not be as intense in their onset, but they are more efficient in their energy transfer to the magnetosphere. Within CIRs, the IMF presents a highly fluctuating southward component (Turner et al., 2006) and thus the geoeffectiveness of CIRs is usually weaker than those of CMEs. In Alves et al. (2006), the geoeffectiveness of CIRs was assessed during the solar wind observational period 1964-2003 and approximately one third of the CIR events observed near the Earth was found geoeffective. The contribution of CIRs and CMEs to geomagnetic activity during the 23rd solar cycle was assessed in Zhang et al. (2008). 

One of the most pronounced differences between CME and CIR driven geomagnetic storms is in their recovery phases (Laughlin et al., 2008).

Title: Distinctive response of thermospheric cooling to ICME and CIR-driven geomagnetic storms
Snippet: In order to understand the average trend of the thermospheric cooling and its response to energy input, we performed a superposed epoch analysis (SEA) study with zero epoch time corresponding to the storm's main phase. The SEA of the CME-and CIR-storms are, respectively, depicted in Figures 2A-E, A1-E1. The horizontal dotted lines represent the pre-onset value. It can clearly see that as the storm intensifies, the thermospheric density also increases both during the CME-and CIR-storms (Figures 2C, C1). The maximum density enhancement occurs within a day of onset, similar to the previous reported results (Lei et al., 2011;Chen et al., 2012;Chen et al., 2104;  and 0.28 mW m −2 for CIR-storm, respectively. This indicates that the impact of the ICME-driven storms is much more than the CIR-driven storms as far as the magnitude is concerned. However, it is interesting to note here that the cooling fluxes take more time (>6-7 days) to recover during CIR-driven storms, whereas, the recovery rate is faster (~3-4 days) for ICME-driven storms. 

In order to understand the impact of the energetic particle precipitations and the energy input from magnetosphere on the thermospheric cooling emission, Figure 3 is presented. Figures 3A-F, A1-F1, respectively, show the DMSP measured electron flux, ion flux along with the Epsilon (ε) and Newell coupling functions (CF) during CME-and CIR-storms. It can be seen that the particle (electron and ion) fluxes and the coupling functions show strong enhancement during both the storm periods. The enhancement in the particle fluxes and the CFs during CME-storm is higher than the CIR-storm. The εparameter shows higher enhancement as compared to the Newell's. The relative enhancement in ε-parameter is more than 50% and 30% during CME-and CIR-storm, respectively, as compared to the quiet value. Whereas, the Newell's CF undergoes enhancement of about 7% and 5%, respectively.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The verification criterion requires the answer to either (1) cite studies that quantify TOTAL/CUMULATIVE transport (flux integrated over storm duration) and state which driver produces greater cumulative transport, OR (2) explicitly acknowledge that existing literature reports only instantaneous flux/peak values without integrated transport calculations. The answer does neither cleanly. Instead, it infers cumulative transport differences from duration and phase-specific flux observations without citing any study that actually performed flux-time integration. For example, it concludes 'CME-driven storms tend to deliver larger...cumulative cold ion transport' and 'CIR-driven storms produce smaller-magnitude but longer-duration cumulative transport' based on combining: (a) CME storms have 'larger density/flux enhancements' [3], (b) CIR storms have 'prolonged recovery' [1], and (c) phase-specific flux snapshots [4,5]. None of the cited references report integrated flux over storm duration. The answer explicitly states in 'Uncertainties' that 'Most inner-magnetosphere flux measurements are event-specific' and 'species-resolved H+/He+/O+ flux integrals...stratified by CIR vs CME would reduce uncertainty,' which implies the cumulative comparison has NOT been directly measured. This acknowledgment should have been the primary answer, not buried in caveats after making definitive cumulative claims.
